title: The Judgment Layer An Inductive Theory of Understanding Synthesis Failure in Large Enterprises

detail.title: The Judgment Layer An Inductive Theory of Understanding Synthesis Failure in Large Enterprises

publicationDetails.detailsText: Thank you for choosing Working Paper submission, we will create a DOI unless one is specified below.

detail.abstract:
Why do large enterprises fail recurrently in domains for which they possess sophisticated operational systems, even after system-level remediation? This empirical pattern, documented across fifteen global organizations spanning six sectors and six geographic regions with aggregate direct financial consequences exceeding USD 80 billion, constitutes an unresolved puzzle in organizational theory.
This paper proposes Judgment Layer Theory (JLT) to explain this pattern. The judgment layer is the institutional architecture, designed or emergent by default, governing how an enterprise synthesizes the collective outputs of its operational systems into documented reasoning at consequential cross-domain decisions. When this architecture is absent, synthesis is informal and leaves no reconstructable institutional artifact. This condition is termed the understanding synthesis gap.
The central theoretical mechanism is as follows: post-failure remediation addresses the system-level deficiencies visible in individual system records without addressing the synthesis gap, which operates above the system level and is therefore invisible to system-level assessment. The structural preconditions for same-category failure are consequently preserved, producing the recurrence pattern. This mechanism is logically distinct from those proposed by organizational learning theory (Argyris and Schon, 1978), high-reliability organization theory (Weick and Sutcliffe, 2001), information processing theory (Galbraith, 1977; Tushman and Nadler, 1978), agency theory (Jensen and Meckling, 1976), and the Viable System Model (Beer, 1972).
Drawing on inductive regulatory document analysis structured through the Gioia methodology (Gioia, Corley, and Hamilton, 2013) and Eisenhardt's (1989) multiple-case logic, the paper develops three falsifiable propositions and a four-category synthesis gap taxonomy. Convergent validation is provided by commercial decision intelligence platform development (Gartner Magic Quadrant, 2024), the EU AI Act's Articles 12 and 13 mandating decision-level traceability, and concurrent academic governance engineering research independently identifying cross-system coupling documentation as the unaddressed gap in decision trace schemas.

title: Does Ambient Heat Impair Elite Sprint Performance? Evidence from 92,000 Track and Field Competitions

detail.title: Does Ambient Heat Impair Elite Sprint Performance? Evidence from 92,000 Track and Field Competitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available athletic performance data and reanalysis weather data. No human subjects were involved and no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We study how ambient heat affects performance in elite sprint athletics using 92,789 outdoor race observations across the 100 m, 200 m, and 400 m events, drawn from the World Athletics performance database spanning 1980-2023. Combining athlete records with ERA5 and MERRA-2 reanalysis weather data, we estimate OLS models with year and event fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the athlete level. We find that heat does not impair, and is marginally associated with faster, sprint times. Using Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT)-the metric adopted by World Athletics for scheduling decisions-races under the "very high risk" threshold of 28 • C are associated with times 0.33 seconds faster (p = 0.006). Within-athlete fixed effects confirm the direction: comparing the same athlete across hot and cool competitions, heat races are 0.03 seconds faster (p = 0.006). Subgroup analysis reveals the performance enhancement is concentrated in the 100 m and 200 m events and among women, while the 400 m-where aerobic metabolism plays a larger role-shows no significant temperature sensitivity. A personal-best gap analysis confirms athletes do not run further below their career ceiling in hot conditions (p = 0.90). These findings diverge sharply from the documented impairment of heat on high-stakes cognitive performance, and are consistent with the physiological distinction between warm-muscle benefits in anaerobic sprint events and heat-induced degradation of executive function. Our results raise questions about whether World Athletics' WBGT-based scheduling thresholds, calibrated primarily for endurance events, apply equally to short-duration sprint competition.

title: What Price Growth? A Bayesian Reappraisal Of Ben Graham's 1949 Valuation Formula
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Record Currency Management

detail.title: What Price Growth? A Bayesian Reappraisal Of Ben Graham's 1949 Valuation Formula
detail.abstract: In his 1949 book The Intelligent Investor, Benjamin Graham gave a littleknown rule that prices an equity from a single input, its expected earnings growth: the price-earnings multiple equals 8.5 + 2G. We reframe the rule as a conditional expectation and study it as a statistical object. Two features emerge. First, the multiplier is affine in the growth rate, so the Bayes price depends on the analyst's growth posterior only through its mean and is completely insensitive to its variance and tails; this is exactly what fails for the discounted-cash-flow value, which is convex in growth and, we show, has infinite posterior expectation whenever growth may approach the discount rate-a Bayesian St. Petersburg paradox in the sense of Durand (1957). Second, a conjugate Gaussian model of log-growth yields a Student-t predictive whose gross-growth mean is infinite (the parameter-uncertainty mechanism of Weitzman, 2007), while a rare-disaster posterior in the manner of Barro (2006) and Gabaix (2012) lowers the posterior-mean growth and makes precise the sense in which Graham's rule is deliberately conservative. We illustrate the framework on NVIDIA. Fitting the growth model to its 2019-2026 earnings, the posterior median one-year growth is 53%, yet the market's price implies a Graham growth of only 11%; the gap is reconciled by an implied 45% posterior probability that hypergrowth normalizes.

title: Factor Heterogeneity in Precious Metals: Why the Right Allocation Depends on what You're Hedging

detail.title: Factor Heterogeneity in Precious Metals: Why the Right Allocation Depends on what You're Hedging

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author declares no conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available market data and does not involve human subjects, animal subjects or sensitive data. No ethics approval was required
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We decompose precious metals returns using vector autoregression (VAR) and generalized forecast error variance decomposition (GFEVD; Pesaran & Shin, 1998) to identify systematic heterogeneity in factor structures across gold, silver, platinum, and palladium. Using monthly CME futures data from 2003-2026 (270 observations after listwise deletion, 10-variable system), we find that own shocks dominate all four metals (51-71%), but the composition of explained variance differs sharply. Gold loads primarily on monetary factors -- real rates (13.5%) and the dollar index (12.6%) -- with negligible sensitivity to inflation expectations (1.6%). White metals (silver, platinum, palladium) exhibit greater sensitivity to supply-side proxies (USD/ZAR: 6-9%), breakeven inflation (5-7%), and risk sentiment (VIX: 2-9%). Traditional industrial demand proxies (vehicle sales, industrial production) explain less than 2% for all metals. This factor heterogeneity has direct portfolio implications: gold's near-zero equity correlation (rho = 0.06 with QQQ) makes it the optimal equity hedge, while white metals' near-zero bond correlation (rho = -0.02 with TLT) makes them effective bond-portfolio diversifiers. An 80/20 QQQ/Gold allocation achieves a Sharpe ratio of 0.94 with 39% maximum drawdown versus 50% for QQQ alone. For bond portfolios, all precious metals blends improve TLT's Sharpe from 0.19 to 0.33-0.34, with no statistically significant difference among them (Jobson-Korkie p > 0.83), but the mechanism differs: white metals load on breakeven inflation with the opposite sign to TLT (beta = +7 to +9 vs. -16.79), so their near-zero bond correlation (rho = -0.02) reflects offsetting factor exposures rather than unrelatedness, while gold shares TLT's real-rates factor (rho = 0.23). Multivariate regressions confirm the sign structure: white metals respond positively and significantly to breakeven inflation (beta = +7 to +9, p < 0.05), while gold's response is statistically indistinguishable from zero (beta = +0.65, p = 0.73) -- consistent with gold's 1.6% inflation variance share and its characterization as a monetary rather than inflation-sensitive metal. Out-of-sample validation across two independent train/test splits confirms that these portfolio findings are not in-sample artifacts: gold remains the best equity complement and all PM blends improve TLT's risk-adjusted return in both holdout periods. These results suggest that "precious metals" is a misleading portfolio category -- the optimal allocation depends on the base asset being hedged.

title: Does Legal access to Handguns Increase Youth Gun Crime? Evidence from Age Discontinuities
affiliations: University of Memphis

detail.title: Does Legal access to Handguns Increase Youth Gun Crime? Evidence from Age Discontinuities
detail.abstract: We know relatively little about the relationship between firearm access and youth involvement in gun crime, particularly for non-fatal crimes. This paper examines the effect of minimum legal age restrictions on handgun possession (MLAG) on juvenile and young adult gun crime. Specifically, I study the federal law that prohibits individuals under the age of 18 from possessing a handgun using a regression discontinuity approach. The results show that the MLAG-18 substantially reduces handgun-related offenses among juveniles. Gun crime rises by approximately 17% at age 18 in MLAG-18 agencies, with fatal gun crime rising by 21% and non-fatal gun crime by 16.5%. Moreover, combining the evidence from both MLAG-18 and MLAG-21 agencies suggests that extending the minimum legal age to 21 could significantly lower handgun crime among individuals aged 18-20.

title: Private Equity Returns: Estimates from 50 Million Funds *
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology - School of Business

detail.title: Private Equity Returns: Estimates from 50 Million Funds *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Do private equity funds compensate investors for illiquidity through superior returns?  We develop and distribute to the public a fully reproducible model of fund returns that allows exact identification of the effects of different treatments on a large number of performance metrics. We simulate 50 million synthetic funds and estimate the full distribution of fund returns under explicitly calibrated cash flow structures, circumventing the sample selection bias, NAV manipulation, and vintage dependence that limit existing empirical estimates. Under the standard 2/20 compensation structure, fewer than 46% of simulated funds outperform a passive public markets equivalent on a raw return basis, with mean underperformance of approximately 1%. However, PE funds exhibit substantially lower return volatility, yielding a risk-adjusted performance twice as large as that of a public markets benchmark. Analyzing the contractual determinants of returns, we find that modifying hurdle rates and carried interests produce modest LP gains but have large, asymmetric effects on GP incentives. Differently, the catch-up provision emerges as the dominant source of distributional distortion. We develop a theoretical model that identifies an interior optimal catch-up parameter of approximately 60\% of the current market practice, robust to LP risk preferences but sensitive to GP effort productivity.

title: Outward Foreign Direct Investment and Domestic Female Employment: Evidence from Korea
affiliations: Hosei University and Guangzhou College of Commerce

detail.title: Outward Foreign Direct Investment and Domestic Female Employment: Evidence from Korea
detail.abstract: This study investigates how foreign direct investment (FDI) affects domestic female employment using unique firm-level data from Korean firms. Unlike most previous studies that focus on the impact of outward-FDI (OFDI) on overall employment growth, this research emphasizes gender-and skill-specific employment outcomes. The findings reveal that OFDI by Korean firms significantly contributed to increases in both total and skilled female employees. Furthermore, the study distinguishes between the impact of OFDI directed toward high-and middle-income countries, showing that OFDI in middle-income countries contributes more to female employment than in high-income countries. Additionally, we find suggestive evidence that the substitution effect between production efficiency and OFDI reduces domestic labor demand, as higher productivity enables firms to produce more with less labor, particularly affecting female workers.

title: When Goliath Shares with David: The Effects of Asymmetry on Collaboration
affiliations: ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research - Junior Research Group Competition and Innovation and Appalachian State University

detail.title: When Goliath Shares with David: The Effects of Asymmetry on Collaboration

declarations.ethicsApproval: University of Texas at Dallas, MR 14-127

detail.abstract: Partners in R&D alliances and joint ventures are rarely symmetric, yet whether asymmetry helps or hurts collaboration is not fully understood. We study how asymmetry in competitors' information endowments affects collaborative knowledge exchange. A model of word-of-mouth communication predicts a clean separation: Initiating the knowledge exchange requires that the informational advantage sacrificed be sufficiently small, while the continuation incentive is independent of the initial endowment (and asymmetry). In a laboratory experiment, we confirm the model's comparative-statics predictions and establish three results. First, initiation rates decline as initial asymmetry increases, holding the better-endowed partner's initial endowment constant. Second, conditional on initiation, the initial asymmetry does not predict defection later in collaboration. Third, extreme asymmetry reduces match length and joint surplus because initiation fails, not because continuation breaks down. The initiation-continuation separation implies that governance mechanisms targeting the formation margin (such as pilot projects, phased disclosure agreements, or credible commitments to reciprocate) can expand the range of asymmetric partnerships that succeed, while continuation requires no special intervention.

title: Optimal COVID restrictions: Is policy making rational during uncertain times?
affiliations: Utrecht University - School of Economics and University College Dublin

detail.title: Optimal COVID restrictions: Is policy making rational during uncertain times?
detail.abstract: Using cross-country variation in policy responses to COVID as a quasi-natural experiment, we provide novel insights on the effect of uncertainty on rational public choice. We propose a simple tractable model in which a government selects the optimal level of policy stringency by minimizing a loss function, comprising the sum of healthcare and economic costs. The model yields a clean characterization of the optimal policy as a function of healthcare burden, economic productivity, and the elasticity of the healthcare system to policy leniency — the latter proxied by societal trust. The model predicts that more responsive policies emerge in low-trust, low-productivity economies. Empirically, we find that governments acted as model-implied optimizing agents during the pandemic, trading off healthcare and economic costs by setting more responsive COVID protocols in countries with lower levels of trust and productivity. However, we find evidence for this optimizing behavior only after the introduction of COVID vaccines. The vaccine rollout served as a critical turning point that reduced ambiguity over policy outcomes, enabling a transition from conservative responses to strategic optimization. The results suggest that there is a threshold of uncertainty beyond which rational public choice is undermined, with potential applications beyond the healthcare sector.

title: Trading on Information versus Trading on Control in Event-Contingent Markets

detail.title: Trading on Information versus Trading on Control in Event-Contingent Markets
detail.abstract: Event-contingent markets trade claims on outcomes (court rulings, mergers, elections, platform-resolved events) that some traders can move, not merely forecast. This paper develops an equilibrium theory of this moral hazard, in which exposure precedes action and trades change the world. With rational dealers, an invariance theorem holds: trading intensity, informativeness, and calibration are unaffected by causal power, which is priced as an identified premium while hedgers finance unbounded real distortion. Manipulation pays only under mechanical liquidity or hidden power. Causal power is derived from governance, organized by a causal Gram matrix, and regulated best by severing feedback, not policing information.

title: Revisiting The Socioeconomic Dimensions of Poverty in Nepal: A Logistic Regression Analysis
affiliations: Tribhuvan University, Florida International University, Tribhuvan University, Tribhuvan University and Tribhuvan University

detail.title: Revisiting The Socioeconomic Dimensions of Poverty in Nepal: A Logistic Regression Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Poverty, a multifaceted concept influenced by several socioeconomic factors, is not only an outcome of individual destiny but also socioeconomically created by severe deprivation of basic needs. Individuals could escape poverty and enhance the quality of life through the government's ample policy interventions. This study examines socioeconomic determinants of poverty in Nepal from multidimensional perspectives. Using household survey data-9600 households-from Nepal Living Standards Survey IV 2022/23, this study applied binary logistic regression analysis. Considering approximately 18% of poor and 82% of nonpoor households, the results revealed the poverty status of households could not be significantly influenced by demographic factors, such as age, gender, and marital status. Rather, poverty status might be influenced by family size, residential status, remittance, nonfarm or side business, agricultural landholdings and livestock, access to electricity, better health and road infrastructure, dwelling status, and preference for cooking fuel. Thus, it is observed that the households may fall into poverty due to higher family dependency, urban residency, agro-landholdings and livestock, firewood as cooking food, availability of the dwelling, and larger family size with the remittance-and that they would walk away from poverty thanks to remittance, family business, electricity, adequate road, and health facilities. This study's findings suggest that nonfarm businesses, less agricultural dependence strategies and programs, and the promotion of physical and social overheads are crucial for achieving Nepal's sustainable development goals by reducing multidimensional poverty.

title: Stable Strategies in Repeated Games with Endogenous Separation
affiliations: and University of Burgos

detail.title: Stable Strategies in Repeated Games with Endogenous Separation

declarations.funderStatement: We thank financial support from the Spanish State Research Agency (PID2024-159461NB-I00/MICIU and PID2020-118906GB-I00/MCIN, AEI/10.13039/501100011033/ EU-FEDER), the Regional Government of Castilla y León and EU-FEDER program (CLU-2019-04 - BIOECOUVA Unit of Excellence of the University of Valladolid), and the Spanish Ministry of Universities (PRX22/00064 and PRX22/00065).

detail.abstract: Games with endogenous separation are repeated games played in a population where players have the option to leave their current partnerships and continue playing in newly formed partnerships. Arguably, most repeated interactions in real life fall into this category. We present a general framework to analyze equilibria in games with endogenous separation, with a focus on neutrally stable strategies, i.e., stable strategies that are resistant to direct invasion by any alternative strategy or small group of strategies. We provide a definition of neutral stability for these games that guarantees dynamic stability properties. We also introduce path-protecting strategies, which play a role similar to that of trigger strategies in standard (fixed-partnership) repeated games. We provide a constructive proof of existence and a Folk Theorem for path-protecting neutrally stable strategies.

title: Means, Methods, and Machine Learning: Toward a "Compliance Review" Framework for AI-Enabled Decision-Support Systems
affiliations: Utrecht University School of Law and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Means, Methods, and Machine Learning: Toward a "Compliance Review" Framework for AI-Enabled Decision-Support Systems
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into military operations, traditional legal review mechanisms face growing interpretive and procedural challenges. Article 36 of Additional Protocol I requires States to determine whether the study, development, acquisition, or adoption of a new weapon, means, or method of warfare would be prohibited under international law. Yet military AI systems, particularly AI-enabled decision-support systems (AI-DSS) and certain autonomous weapons systems (AWS), do not fit neatly within conventional understandings of these reviews. While such systems may not directly apply force, they can materially influence targeting decisions, threat assessments, collateral damage estimations, and other functions central to the conduct of hostilities. This article argues that the challenges posed by military AI cannot be addressed through a static, end-stage interpretation of Article 36 review alone. Instead, Article 36 should be situated within a broader lifecycle-based "compliance review" framework grounded in the preventive and protective purposes of international humanitarian law (IHL). Drawing on a functional approach, the article contends that legal scrutiny should focus not on whether a system formally qualifies as a weapon, but on whether its functions materially affect compliance with IHL obligations relating to distinction, precautions, proportionality and accountability. Building on emerging discussions within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (CCW GGE LAWS), recent military AI governance initiatives, and responsible-by-design approaches to AI assurance, the article develops a model of continuous compliance review extending across system conception, design, data governance, testing and evaluation, procurement, deployment, operational use, monitoring, modification, and retirement. The proposed framework integrates Article 36 with broader obligations arising from common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions and related IHL provisions that require States not merely to assess legality ex ante but to ensure ongoing compliance in practice. The article concludes that a lifecycle-based compliance review model provides a more effective mechanism for aligning military AI innovation with the preventive, accountability-enhancing, and civilian-protective purposes of international humanitarian law.

title: An Anti-noise and High-precision TDOA Positioning Framework for Underwater Acoustic Localization
affiliations: Guangdong Ocean University, Guangdong Ocean University, Guangdong University of Technology and Guangdong Ocean University

detail.title: An Anti-noise and High-precision TDOA Positioning Framework for Underwater Acoustic Localization
detail.abstract: Underwater acoustic positioning is a core technology for current underwater target localization. In the highly dynamic marine environment, underwater acoustic positioning is subject to numerous noise interferences. However, existing theoretical models based on static assumptions deviate significantly from dynamic real-world marine scenarios, and suffer from high energy consumption in time-varying systems. To address these issues, a tdoa-based accurate positioning and learning (TAPL) scheme is constructed in this paper.First, the scheme is established based on the Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) measurement method. On the one hand, the Integration-Enhanced Zeroing Neural Network (IEZNN) is adopted, and an error-adaptive adjustment factor is introduced to solve the inverse problem of TDOA positioning for buoy networks, thereby achieving high-precision and high-robustness positioning. On the other hand, the Recursive Least Squares (RLS) algorithm is employed to estimate and update the pseudo-inverse of the buoy Jacobian matrix using real-time data, which avoids the time consumption caused by analytical modeling of buoys and the direct computation of the Jacobian matrix and its pseudo-inverse in each iteration.Finally, the feasibility, accuracy and robustness of the proposed localization scheme are verified through theoretical analysis and simulations. Moreover, a series of comparative experiments are conducted to highlight the superior performance of the proposed scheme.

title: Singapore's Corporate Governance Paradox: Lessons from Three Systemic Failures*
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Singapore's Corporate Governance Paradox: Lessons from Three Systemic Failures*

contentType.other: Draft for a chapter in a book

detail.abstract: Singapore's reputation as a premier financial hub rests on robust regulation, transparency, and investor protection. Yet beneath this institutional strength lie vulnerabilities capable of significant corporate failure. This chapter examines three—the collapse of Hyflux Limited, the fraud at Hin Leong Trading, and nominee directorship abuses in Public Prosecutor v Zheng Jia—spanning public market failure, private company fraud, and criminal exploitation of the incorporation regime. Three themes emerge: reputational "halo effects" operating at firm, ecosystem, and jurisdictional levels; the limits of a predominantly reactive enforcement model; and a persistent disjunction between formal compliance and substantive governance effectiveness. The chapter argues that doctrinal adequacy alone is insufficient. Strengthening Singapore's regime requires recalibrating the balance between facilitation and control—moving from reactive enforcement toward anticipatory supervision, from formalistic compliance toward functional oversight, and from reputation-based trust toward verification grounded in data, monitoring, and accountability.

title: Strategic OTC Market Making with Reputation Feedback
affiliations: HSBC FX eRisk, Global Markets, HSBC Bank Plc., UK

detail.title: Strategic OTC Market Making with Reputation Feedback
detail.abstract: Electronic over-the-counter (OTC) liquidity provision is increasingly shaped not only by the price of the next quote, but also by a dealer's accumulated standing with clients and platforms. We develop a stochastic-control model in which request-for-quote (RFQ) win ratios and streaming fill ratios feed back into future flow through performance-based flow gates, creating an explicit trade-off between immediate spread capture and long-term franchise value. The resulting policy naturally alternates between reputation-building campaigns and franchise monetization phases, and can generate multiple stable client-flow regimes even in a parsimonious single dealer control problem.

title: Groundwater Depletion and Institutions: Exploring the Colonial Origin
affiliations: IFMR Graduate School of Business, Krea University - IFMR Graduate School of Business, Krea University, Students and IFMR Graduate School of Business, Krea University - IFMR Graduate School of Business, Krea University, Students

detail.title: Groundwater Depletion and Institutions: Exploring the Colonial Origin
detail.abstract: Taking a global perspective, this study empirically examines how the institutional structures established during the colonial period continue to impact modern groundwater outcomes. Combining data from multiple sources such as GLDAS, the Fraser Institute, the Economic Intelligence Unit, the World Bank, IGRAC, and the NASA Earth Data System, we compile an exhaustive novel dataset of geospatial and institutional variables covering 64 countries from 2003 to 2019. We examine the role of institutional quality—measured through the Property Rights Index and the Democracy Index—in shaping contemporary groundwater levels. We employ an instrumental variable approach in two stages to address potential endogeneity in institutional measures: stage one uses geographical variables to predict the incidence of colonization, and stage two uses predicted values from stage one as instruments for the protection of property rights index and democracy index to determine groundwater levels. Our results reveal a relationship between institutional quality and groundwater levels: improvements in property rights and democratic accountability are associated with a 351.35mm and 177.520mm rise in groundwater levels, respectively. However, these better groundwater outcomes show up to a point, beyond which diminishing returns become apparent. Climate variables, such as average temperature and precipitation, play a role but are far less influential than institutional characteristics. Overall, the study demonstrates that the groundwater crisis is not only an environmental or climatic issue, but also a long-standing institutional one, deeply rooted in colonial history.

detail.abstract: This paper examines real estate as a mechanism for wealth accumulation in two structurally distinct economies: the United States, a mature, highly financialized housing market, and India, a rapidly liberalizing emerging market. Drawing on a synthesis of empirical literature on housing wealth effects, long-run wealth-income ratios, housing affordability, and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs), the review finds that housing wealth effects in emerging market economies are broadly comparable in magnitude to those in advanced economies, and that real estate remains the dominant component of household wealth in both contexts despite very different institutional and financing environments. To complement the literature review with primary evidence, the study administered a structured cross-national survey to 30 respondents residing in the United States (n = 15) and India (n = 15). Descriptive and inferential analysis of the survey data shows nearuniversal agreement (90-100%) that real estate builds long-term wealth and increases financial security, alongside persistent barriers to entry: only 30% of respondents personally own real estate, 46.7% report difficulty obtaining a mortgage or home loan, and only 33.3% have heard of REITs. Cross-national comparisons using chi-square and Fisher's exact tests found no statistically significant difference between the two countries on most measures at the 5% level, though Indian respondents reported directionally higher difficulty accessing mortgage credit (66.7% vs. 26.7% in the U.S.; p = 0.066, Fisher's exact), consistent with the literature's emphasis on India's comparatively shallow mortgage market. The findings reinforce that, while belief in real estate as a wealth-building vehicle is nearly universal across both markets, structural barriers to access, capital, and financial-instrument literacy constrain its realization, with REITs offering a promising yet under-recognized pathway to democratization.

title: Machine Learning and Computer Vision Applications in Ultrasound Image Analysis

detail.abstract: Ultrasound imaging is one of the most widely used diagnostic modalities in modern healthcare because of its non-invasive nature, real-time imaging capability, affordability, and absence of ionizing radiation. Despite these advantages, ultrasound images are often affected by speckle noise, low contrast, and operator-dependent variability, which can reduce diagnostic accuracy and complicate clinical interpretation. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and computer vision (CV), have significantly enhanced the automated analysis of ultrasound images by improving image quality, feature extraction, segmentation, classification, and disease detection. This study presents a systematic literature synthesis of contemporary research on ML and CV applications in ultrasound image analysis, drawing on recent developments in deep learning, vision transformers, transfer learning, and intelligent image processing. The review examines existing methodologies, clinical applications, and emerging technologies while comparing their strengths and limitations across different diagnostic domains. The findings indicate that deep learning-based computer vision models consistently outperform conventional image analysis techniques in tasks such as lesion detection, organ segmentation, fetal assessment, lung ultrasound interpretation, and disease classification. Furthermore, advances in transfer learning and transformer-based architectures have improved model robustness and generalization, although challenges related to data availability, model interpretability, computational requirements, and clinical integration remain. The study concludes that AI-driven ultrasound image analysis has considerable potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making. Future research should prioritize explainable AI, multimodal learning, standardized datasets, edge-based deployment, and rigorous clinical validation to facilitate safe and widespread adoption in healthcare practice.

Johnson, V.C. (2026). Building Trustworthy AI Governance for Critical Infrastructure: Foundations of the European–African Governance Adaptation Framework (EA-AGAF). EA-AGAF Research Series, Vol. I. Zenodo. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21315097

detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the governance of critical infrastructure by enabling intelligent decision-making, predictive analytics, automation, and operational optimisation across sectors including energy, healthcare, transportation, finance, telecommunications, and public administration. While these technologies offer significant opportunities for innovation and resilience, they also introduce complex governance challenges relating to accountability, transparency, cybersecurity, privacy, ethics, regulatory compliance, organisational capability, and public trust. Existing AI governance frameworks provide valuable principles and regulatory guidance but are frequently designed within specific institutional and legal contexts, limiting their direct applicability across regions with differing governance maturity and implementation capacities.

This publication establishes the conceptual foundations of the European–African Governance Adaptation Framework (EA-AGAF), an adaptive governance approach that integrates internationally recognised principles of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence with context-sensitive implementation mechanisms suitable for diverse institutional environments. Drawing upon a comparative analysis of international AI governance initiatives—including those of the OECD, UNESCO, the European Union, the African Union, ISO/IEC, and NIST—the study examines the evolution of AI governance, the convergence of global governance principles, and the distinct governance trajectories of Europe and Africa. The analysis further explores the growing integration of AI governance with cybersecurity governance, digital resilience, enterprise governance, and critical infrastructure protection.

The publication argues that effective AI governance depends not solely on regulatory sophistication but on organisations' ability to adapt governance principles to their institutional realities while strengthening governance maturity, cybersecurity capability, organisational resilience, and continuous learning. On this basis, the study introduces the conceptual philosophy, design principles, governance domains, implementation cycle, strategic outcomes, and research roadmap of the European–African Governance Adaptation Framework. Rather than replacing existing governance frameworks, EA-AGAF is proposed as a complementary governance model that facilitates the adaptive implementation of internationally recognised AI governance principles across different governance ecosystems.

As the inaugural volume of the EA-AGAF Research Series, this publication provides the theoretical and conceptual foundation for a broader programme of research that will develop governance architecture, maturity assessment models, implementation methodologies, sector-specific applications, and empirical validation studies. The work contributes to the growing body of scholarship on trustworthy Artificial Intelligence by advancing adaptive governance as a practical strategy for strengthening cybersecurity governance, digital resilience, and responsible AI deployment within critical infrastructure.

keywords.keywords: Internal controls; fraud prevention; fraud detection; corporate governance; COSO framework; financial institutions; data analytics; machine learning; regulatory compliance; audit committees.

detail.abstract: Financial fraud remains a constant and evolving threat to U.S. financial institutions, damaging market integrity, diminishing public trust, and causing significant economic losses. Internal control systems serve as the first line of defense against such fraud, yet many institutions still face control failures that allow internal and external schemes to thrive. Despite comprehensive regulatory requirements and compliance measures, fraud incidents persist, highlighting ongoing weaknesses in the design and execution of internal controls. This underscores the need for stronger, technology-driven prevention strategies. This research analyzes the effectiveness of internal control systems in preventing and detecting fraud in U.S. financial institutions. It proposes an integrated framework combining governance mechanisms, risk assessment, technological advancements, and human capital development to improve fraud deterrence. The study uses an applied qualitative approach to systematically review and compare evidence from academic journals, government reports, banking regulations, and industry publications.

title: The Assistant is not the Population
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Assistant is not the Population
detail.abstract: Social simulation asks a language model to reproduce distributions of human behavior: what a population answers, how a group negotiates, which number a person picks. We treat this distributional fidelity as a training outcome and measure it stage by stage across post-training. Using seven public OLMo 3 7B checkpoints spanning a shared pretrained base and complete reasoning and chat pipelines, we evaluate 7,167 questions with published human answer distributions, economic games, random-number generation, and 875 multi-agent negotiations. Exact candidate scoring and token-level constrained decoding give every checkpoint, including the base, one instrument with zero format failures. On the primary human-referenced battery, all six post-trained checkpoints score below the base (mean representativeness, a 0-1 fidelity score, of 0.799 at the base against 0.737 at the final chat checkpoint, dataset-level intervals disjoint); the chat pipeline declines at every stage, and the reasoning pipeline never returns to the base level. Across four recipes on three pretrained lineages, only one transition repeats in direction: every supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to direct preference optimization (DPO) step lowers fidelity, from-0.005 to-0.074 depending on recipe, robust to dataset-level resampling in three, and the same point estimate at 7B and 32B within OLMo. At 7B the two pipelines fail differently: reasoning training concentrates behavior onto narrow modes while chat training flattens it, so an entropy audit of single-draw behavior would rank the chat pipeline highest even though its endpoint is the least survey-faithful OLMo checkpoint we measure. No checkpoint, the base included, is a certified human sampler. But the comparison never flips: in every recipe we measure, post-training pulls the model further from the population it is asked to simulate.

title: From Checkout to Clicks: SNAP Online Purchase Pilot Program and Food Security

detail.title: From Checkout to Clicks: SNAP Online Purchase Pilot Program and Food Security

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflict of interest to disclose.

detail.abstract: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Online Purchasing Pilot (OPP) represents a major shift in how SNAP households can redeem food benefits, yet its effects on food security remain unclear. This study examines the short‑run impact of the OPP on food security among low‑income households using the Survey of Income and Program Participation from 2019 to 2021. Using the staggered timing of OPP adoption across states, this paper employs a weighted stacked difference‑in‑differences design. The main results show no statistically detectable effect of OPP availability on household food security during the first two months following implementation. Subgroup analyses also yield null effects. These results differ from prior evidence showing reductions in food insufficiency during the similar period. Future work incorporating longer post‑implementation horizons and measures of digital access will be essential for understanding the longer‑term implications of online benefit redemption.

title: Modeling Economic Impacts of a Hyperscale Data Center Campus
affiliations: Capital University - School of Management and Indiana University Bloomington - School of Public & Environmental Affairs (SPEA)

detail.title: Modeling Economic Impacts of a Hyperscale Data Center Campus

declarations.funderStatement: The authors appreciate funding support for this project from the Northwest Indiana Forum. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the Northwest Indiana Forum.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a conservative framework for estimating the regional economic impacts of hyperscale data-center campuses. Data-center projects present a difficult measurement problem because announced capital investment often includes imported IT equipment, land transfers, out-of-region vendors, nonlocal utility inputs, and construction labor that may not reside in the study region. Using Northwest Indiana as a case study, we apply BEA RIMS II multipliers to three hypothetical hyperscale data center campus configurations: 0.5 gigawatts, 1 gigawatt, and 1.5 gigawatts, corresponding to $5 billion, $10 billion, and $15 billion in capital investment. For the 1 gigawatt illustrative case, the construction phase is estimated to support approximately $5.45 billion in regional output, $1.08 billion in earnings, and 14,651 job-years over a three-year build via direct and indirect effects (Type I). Including induced household-spending effects (Type II) raises the estimate to approximately $6.72 billion in output, $1.34 billion in earnings, and 20,133 job-years. Once operational, the 1 gigawatt campus is estimated to support approximately $691 million in annual regional output, $176 million in annual earnings, and 2,090 jobs on a Type I basis. Including induced effects, the supplementary Type II estimate rises to approximately $846 million in annual output, $219 million in annual earnings, and 2,986 jobs. Relative to the broader RIMS II direct-employment count, which includes on-site staff as well as directly engaged contract and vendor workers, the operations estimates imply employment multipliers of approximately 2.26 on a Type I basis and 3.22 on a Type II basis.

title: How Much Does Each Modality Matter? An Empirical Study of Market, Macro-Financial, and Text Signals in Short-Horizon Equity Volatility Forecasting

detail.title: How Much Does Each Modality Matter? An Empirical Study of Market, Macro-Financial, and Text Signals in Short-Horizon Equity Volatility Forecasting
detail.abstract: Multimodal machine learning is widely reported to improve financial forecasting, yet the incremental value of each modality is rarely quantified under a common, strictly out-of-sample protocol. This paper constructs a fully public multimodal dataset for the S&P 500 covering January 2015 to July 2026 (2,879 trading days) that combines (i) a market modality built from daily open, high, low, close, and volume data, including Garman-Klass realized volatility and heterogeneous autoregressive terms, (ii) a macro-financial modality comprising the VIX, the ten-year Treasury yield, and the broad dollar index, and (iii) a text modality comprising the daily newspaper-based Economic Policy Uncertainty index and Loughran-McDonald tone extracted from 98 Federal Open Market Committee statements. Five model classes are evaluated on five-day-ahead realized volatility with expanding-window annual refits over 882 test days (January 2023 to July 2026). Adding macrofinancial information to a heterogeneous autoregressive baseline raises out-of-sample R 2 from 0.299 to 0.369 and lowers the QLIKE loss by 12.4 percent, with gains concentrated in the turbulent 2025 episode, although Diebold-Mariano tests do not reject equal pooled accuracy at conventional levels. Text features add no incremental accuracy once implied volatility is included, and flexible nonlinear learners underperform regularized linear models at this sample size, with the widest neural specification significantly worse than the baseline. The evidence suggests that option-implied volatility already subsumes most policy-related text information at the daily horizon, and that in moderate-sample financial settings modality selection matters more than model complexity.

title: A Theory of International Official Lending
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, Tsinghua University and Emory University

detail.title: A Theory of International Official Lending
detail.abstract: Official lending is large, senior, and countercyclical, continuing after sovereigns fall into arrears on private debt. We ask why sovereign finance exhibits this division of labor across creditors. In a production economy where a risk-averse sovereign privately allocates imported inputs, commitment is limited on both sides, and monitoring generates a noisy signal, the constrained-optimal allocation is decentralized by defaultable private debt, senior nondefaultable multilateral debt, and concessional bilateral debt whose relief is tied to the signal. Production remains distorted, but the sovereign is never excluded: official lending is monitored liquidity provision. A calibration reproduces procyclical private and countercyclical official debt.

title: Resistance or Aggression? The Battle of Narratives Behind the Israel-Hezbollah Conflict in Lebanon

detail.title: Resistance or Aggression? The Battle of Narratives Behind the Israel-Hezbollah Conflict in Lebanon
detail.abstract: This case study examines the Israel–Hezbollah conflict in Lebanon through the Change-Oriented Conflict Analysis framework, with particular attention to the competing narratives that shape how the conflict is understood and sustained. Drawing on peer-reviewed scholarship, reports from international organizations, and a comparative narrative analysis of official statements between October 2023 and mid-2026, the study explores how Hezbollah, Israel, and the Lebanese state frame the conflict through the lenses of resistance, security, sovereignty, and civilian protection. The analysis identifies the conflict's historical roots in Israeli occupation, the Palestinian issue, weak Lebanese state institutions, regional alliances, and competing collective memories. It also examines the interests of key stakeholders, cultural considerations, and theethical dilemmas surrounding civilian protection, accountability, and the use of force. The findings demonstrate that the conflict remains highly intractable because each actor defines the problem, responsibility, and legitimate solutionsdifferently, reinforcing cycles of violence and limiting opportunities for compromise. While no single intervention can resolve the conflict, the study argues that stronger implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1701, greater support for Lebanese state institutions, improved civilian protection, sustained diplomatic engagement, and narrative-sensitive conflict management could reduce escalation and create conditions for longer-term de-escalation. Ultimately, durable peace requires addressing not only military and territorial disputes but also the competing narratives and unresolved political questions that continue to drive the conflict.

title: Modeling the Interactions Between Zero-Day Options and Underlying Markets Using Joint Limit Order Book Data
affiliations: Purdue University - College of Science and University of Washington

detail.title: Modeling the Interactions Between Zero-Day Options and Underlying Markets Using Joint Limit Order Book Data
detail.abstract: We propose a framework to quantify intraday cross-market interactions between zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options and their underlying exchange-traded funds (ETFs) using event-level data. A joint limit order book model is developed to estimate event intensities, such as order arrivals, cancellations, and trades, via a multivariate Hawkes process. We find statistically significant cross-market excitation and strong same-market clustering, with interactions that are asymmetric and highly time-varying over the trading day. Distinct patterns in interaction strength are observed around macroeconomic announcements. The framework further identifies microstructure-level drivers of cross-market excitation, allowing different event types to be decomposed, quantified, and compared in terms of their contributions to cross-market dynamics.

title: On the Efficiency of Inspection Targeting
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management and University of California, San Diego

detail.title: On the Efficiency of Inspection Targeting
detail.abstract: Enforcement agencies are often evaluated on detected violations, yet the ultimate goal of enforcement is to reduce misconduct. We show theoretically that these objectives diverge when firms differ in their propensity to misbehave. Targeting high-risk firms yields immediate detections, but misconduct then accumulates among the low-risk firms left unmonitored, so a regulator rewarded for detection targets high-risk firms excessively. A budget cut separates the two objectives: prevention-oriented enforcement widens the misconduct gap between high-and low-risk firms, whereas a narrowing gap is a signature that prevention cannot produce. The mechanism is common to other enforcement settings, and better prediction can deepen rather than resolve the misallocation. We take the model to Cal/OSHA around the 2009 California budget crisis and find that the cross-industry accident gradient flattened after the cut, consistent with detection maximization at the expense of prevention.

title: Lands Reclaimed: Additions to Reserve and Indigenous Economic Development
affiliations: ,  and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Lands Reclaimed: Additions to Reserve and Indigenous Economic Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: The Canadian federal government introduced an Additions to Reserve (ATR) policy in 1972 to facilitate the expansion of land holdings by First Nations. In subsequent decades, Indigenous nations have engaged in hundreds of additions, either by expanding existing reserves, or creating new ones. We consider the impact of these additions on the well-being of Indigenous nations by marrying data on ATRs to data from the Censuses of Population. We find that the effects of additions to reserve depend on the permissiveness of the policy regime, and the type of reserve added. While additions to reserve generally appear to have negligible impact on First Nations' socioeconomic outcomes, urban reserves added since the mid-1990s, when the policy became less restrictive, are associated with economically significant improvements in socioeconomic outcomes. Our results point to the substantial value of urban reserves to Indigenous nations and suggest that government restrictions may have undermined potential gains of ATRs.

title: Informational Distance and Present Value: A Structural Decomposition

detail.title: Informational Distance and Present Value: A Structural Decomposition
detail.abstract: The interest rate is commonly understood as the intertemporal price of money. This note decomposes that price into two components: the price of waiting, r w , and the price of the unknown, r u. The price of waiting has a natural time dimension: it compensates for loss of purchasing power, forgone growth, and productive opportunity. The price of the unknown is different. It compensates for opacity, weak verification, monitoring difficulty, enforcement risk, illiquidity, and institutional fragility. Its relevant exposure is not calendar time alone, but informational distance. In the conventional formula, P V = F V /(1 + r) t , the combined rate r = r w + r u (D) is compounded over calendar time. This can bias valuation when the unknown component is applied over t even though the relevant informational exposure is D. The note proposes the structural expression P V S = F V /[(1 + r w) t (1 + r u) D ]. Informational distance is represented heuristically as D = B/K, where B is informational burden and K is institutional capacity. The decomposition clarifies the valuation of long-horizon projects, the shift from fixed distance premia toward participation-based contracts, and the distribution of information rents. It also makes the information-generating process explicit, suggesting that macro-financial coordination may operate not only through the interest rate, but also through institutions that reduce B, increase K, and compress D.

title: Replicating and Optimizing the S&P 500 BuyWrite Index: A Market Microstructure Decomposition of ETF Tracking Error

detail.title: Replicating and Optimizing the S&P 500 BuyWrite Index: A Market Microstructure Decomposition of ETF Tracking Error
detail.abstract: We examine the market microstructure of the Invesco S&P 500 BuyWrite ETF (PBP), which tracks the Cboe S&P 500 BuyWrite Index (BXM). Using 14.8 gigabytes of Cboe SPX options tick data for 2022, we make three contributions. First, adopting the expiry-to-expiry return methodology of Kumiega et al. [2024], we reduce the apparent annualized tracking error from 4.80% (daily Nasdaq close) to 0.93% (R 2 = 0.9963), consistent with Bloomberg's reported figure of 1.334%. Second, we decompose the remaining tracking error into three structural components: VWAP execution slippage (-1.41%/year, 55% of total), the fund expense ratio (-0.29%, 11%), and execution residual attributable to smearing and sampling (-0.87%, 34%). The decomposition is exact by construction. Third, we implement a dynamic switching algorithm based on the implied volatility-realized volatility (IV-RV) spread. When IV exceeds RV, we sell at-the-money calls (BXM strategy); otherwise we sell 30-delta calls (BXMD strategy). In 2022, the dynamic strategy achieves an annualized return of-3.72% with a Return-to-Risk ratio of-0.217, outperforming static BXM (-7.65%,-0.531) and the PBP ETF itself (-10.21%,-0.668). Results are directionally consistent with Kumiega et al. [2024], though limited to a single bear-market year (N = 11).

title: Algorithmic Panic or Inherited Beta? Asymmetric Volatility and Tail Risk of AI-managed ETFs Across the 2024 U.S. Presidential Transition

detail.title: Algorithmic Panic or Inherited Beta? Asymmetric Volatility and Tail Risk of AI-managed ETFs Across the 2024 U.S. Presidential Transition
detail.abstract: The global financial architecture experienced a stochastic regime shift between 2024 and 2026, driven by heightened geopolitical uncertainty during the U.S. electoral transition and the subsequent post-2024 election administration. During this period, market volatility decoupled from traditional macroeconomic fundamentals, generating extreme price fluctuations across equities, commodities, and digital assets. This paper investigates the tail risk and asymmetric volatility of 15 major assets, directly contrasting Artificial Intelligence (AI) managed ETFs, human-managed innovation funds, passive market indexes, and decentralized digital assets. Using an EGARCH (1,1) specification with a Student-t distribution, an Extreme Value Theory (EVT) framework combining block-maxima GEV and Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT/GPD) models, and dynamic structural-break tests, we analyze daily returns over an extended sample from January 2022 to June 2026 that includes a pre-transition baseline. The central result is that the asymmetric "leverage effect" exhibited by AI-managed ETFs is not an intrinsic algorithmic property but an inherited market-beta exposure: once returns are orthogonalized against the S&P 500, the idiosyncratic leverage coefficient is statistically insignificant for every managed fund. AI ETFs behave as closet indexers (marketmodel R² up to 0.94), and their tail behavior is largely indistinguishable from the benchmark they shadow. A properly specified EVT analysis shows that a naive Gumbel fit to the daily-loss distribution is rejected by goodness-of-fit tests for all assets; the free-shape GEV selects the heavier-tailed Fréchet domain for 14 of 15 assets, and POT/GPD Value-at-Risk (with bootstrap confidence intervals) confirms that Gaussian models understate one-day 99% tail losses across AI funds and crypto-assets. Finally, endogenous break tests locate the structural adjustment weeks after the event dates, indicating a lagged rather than instantaneous market response. These findings temper the "algorithmic coldness" narrative and reframe the risk of AI-managed products as one of dependence on structural benchmarks.

title: Intergenerational Spillovers of Birth Order: Evidence from the United States
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: Intergenerational Spillovers of Birth Order: Evidence from the United States
detail.abstract: Birth order shapes life outcomes, but do these differences persist across generations? This paper examines whether a mother's birth order is associated with her children's developmental trajectories. Using mother-child panel data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, I find that children of later-born mothers score lower on cognitive tests than those of firstborn mothers. These gaps emerge early, persist into adolescence, and are associated with lower college completion. In magnitude, these intergenerational differences are about one-third the size of canonical first-generation birth order gaps. Suggestive evidence indicates that children of later-born mothers receive less cognitive and emotional stimulation at home than those of firstborn mothers.

title: When Volatility Targeting Thins the Tail: A Forecast-quality Law

detail.title: When Volatility Targeting Thins the Tail: A Forecast-quality Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: That volatility targeting thins return tails is well documented at the level of momentsskewness, kurtosis-and drawdown; what has been missing is a mechanism, stated at the level of the tail index itself. Writing a heteroscedastic return as the product of a predictable volatility and an independent shock, in the spirit of Breiman, the loss-tail shape parameter is the heavier of the two factor tails: a volatility tail and an innovation tail. In a GARCH model the volatility tail is endogenous and empirically dominant, and dividing the return by a predictable volatility forecast cancels that factor, leaving the innovation tail as a floor that, as we prove, no volatility overlay can breach: the reduction is 𝛥𝜉 = (𝜉 𝜎-𝜉 𝜀) + in closed form. A forecast-quality law, 𝜉 𝜀 ̂= 𝑚𝑎𝑥(𝜉 𝑄 , 𝜉 𝜀), makes the residual tail a function of the tail of the forecast-error ratio 𝜎 𝜎 ⁄ : a responsive forecast keeps the ratio bounded and the managed tail at the innovation floor; a forecast that lags a volatility jump lets the ratio spike and the tail fatten. Across seventeen markets the prediction holds in every case (Wilcoxon p < 0.0001), with the mean loss-tail index falling from 0.18 to 0.06 under a simple real-time overlay (trailing 21-day volatility, de-lever only) and to 0.03 under a GARCH forecast, the 99% Expected Shortfall approximately halved, and the model-implied tail ordering matching the measured one. Slowing the forecast reverses the gain, exactly as the law predicts.

title: Closing the AI Audit Gap: Forensic Design Requirements for AI-driven Security Operations

detail.title: Closing the AI Audit Gap: Forensic Design Requirements for AI-driven Security Operations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: no human subjects, no patients, no participants.

detail.abstract: AI-driven security operations create a forensic accountability problem that existing readiness frameworks were not designed to address. SIEM triage, SOAR playbooks, and agentic investigation tools now make or in luence security decisions at machine speed, yet they typically log outcomes rather than reasoning; when an AI action is later questioned by an investigator, a regulator, or a court, the record is often insuf icient to reconstruct what was decided, by which model version, on what inputs, and why. This article identi ies ive structural gaps that AI participation introduces into cloud security operations (attribution, decision opacity, model drift, shadow AI, and adversarial automation) and derives ive corresponding design requirements for auditable AI: decision logging, agentic chain tracing, model version forensics, shadow AI discovery, and an adversarial automation escalation protocol. The requirements are grounded in an integrative review of the forensic readiness literature and structured practitioner observation in a regulated enterprise environment, and they are stated as actionable design inputs for security architects. Regulatory context (NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, SEC disclosure requirements) and a phased adoption path support implementation before, rather than after, the next incident.

title: The Economics of Digital Transactions
affiliations: Indian School of Business, Indian School of Business,  and UCLA Anderson

detail.title: The Economics of Digital Transactions
detail.abstract: Are digital transactions cheaper than cash? Using India's Unified Payments Interface as our laboratory, we show that digital payments dominate cash on cost grounds at virtually all transaction sizes once fixed infrastructure is amortized. A modified cashin-advance model formalizes how rising digital adoption increases velocity-requiring the central bank to tighten money supply beyond its inflation target by a computable correction factor. Digitization further expands credit access through verifiable digital income records and generates large time savings from eliminating physical cash management. Policy implications for fee design, cross-subsidization, and currency issuance follow directly.

title: Public Expenditure Efficiency and Sustainable Development Outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa: Evidence from Nigeria and Comparator Economies

detail.title: Public Expenditure Efficiency and Sustainable Development Outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa: Evidence from Nigeria and Comparator Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary data from the World Bank World Development Indicators, IMF Government Finance Statistics, and related international databases. No human subjects, patients, or participants were involved. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently as part of the author's academic research programme at Lagos State University, Nigeria.

detail.abstract:
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development has intensified global scrutiny of whether
public expenditure generates commensurate progress toward the Sustainable Development
Goals (SDGs). This paper examines the efficiency of public expenditure in producing
SDG-relevant development outcomes — specifically poverty reduction (SDG 1), economic
growth and employment (SDG 8), and infrastructure development (SDG 9) — across Nigeria
and ten structurally comparable Sub-Saharan African economies over the period 2005–2022.
Using a two-stage analytical framework combining Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with
Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression with HC1 heteroskedasticity-consistent robust
standard errors, we produce bias-corrected government efficiency scores and identify the
institutional and macroeconomic determinants of efficiency variation across the panel. The
DEA model is implemented in Python 3.12 using the HiGHS LP solver (SciPy), with data
drawn from the World Bank World Development Indicators, IMF Government Finance
Statistics, World Bank CPIA database, and the Database of Political Institutions.
Results reveal striking heterogeneity. Kenya, Ghana, and Ethiopia achieve near-frontier
mean efficiency scores of 0.920, consistently converting their expenditure into the maximum
achievable SDG output given sample production possibilities. Nigeria records the lowest
mean efficiency of 0.372 — delivering only 37 per cent of the SDG output its expendi-
ture level should theoretically support. Angola (0.615) and Zambia (0.574) also perform
significantly below the sample mean of 0.758. The Tobit-approximation regression (OLS
with HC1 robust SE, R2 = 0.607) identifies resource revenue dependence (β = −0.0052,
p < 0.001), capital expenditure share (β = 0.0043, p < 0.05), and institutional quality
(β = 0.054, p < 0.10) as the dominant determinants of efficiency variation. Electoral year
effects are negative but statistically insignificant. The findings have direct implications for
fiscal reform, SDG financing design, and the sequencing of public financial management
reforms ahead of the 2030 deadline.

Decomposing Commercial Property Prices into Land, Structure, and Dynamic Spatial Components 
An Adaptive Delaunay-Grid Hedonic for Tokyo's 23 Special Wards, 2015-2024 *

detail.abstract: We decompose commercial property values into a metropolitan land-price index α t , a static spatial level θ c over an adaptive Delaunay grid, a corner-by-year interaction ψ c,t , and a structure-price index β t , identied by penalised non-linear least squares with spatial Laplacians on log θ and log ψ c,t. The anchor ψ c,2015 = 1 and the gauge c ω c log ψc,t = 0 identify α t as an exact xed-weight Jevons index of corner-level land-price relatives, consistent in two-stage geometric aggregation over wards. We construct a J-REIT working panel of 8,073 property-year observations on 1,063 Oce and Apartment properties from Tokyo's 23 special wards over 20152024; the four-model estimation panel, after requiring strictly positive reported structure age, contains 7,083 observations on 933 properties. We benchmark DSG-PM against ward-dummy specications with exogenous and endogenous structure prices. The dynamic block recovers cumulative ψc,2024 ranges of 0.482.74 (Oce) and 0.481.79 (Apartment) around an exposure-weighted geometric mean of one, identifying within-ward spatial-temporal heterogeneity that static specications cannot express.

title: Toward a Corporate AMT Singularity: Book Income with Tax Characteristics
affiliations: Fried Frank

detail.title: Toward a Corporate AMT Singularity: Book Income with Tax Characteristics
detail.abstract:
The corporate alternative minimum tax (AMT) imposes a 15 percent minimum tax on a corporation’s financial statement income) with certain tax-related adjustments. Its 2022 enactment was the culmination of almost four decades of efforts by tax law professors at Yale Law School and other academic research institutions.

The federal government has been issuing corporate AMT guidance at a rate of around one page per day. Meanwhile, the federal government’s tax law and financial accounting experts have shown that the corporate AMT is taxing fewer corporations over time and may tax none before the end of 2027 under current trends.

This article analyzes the ratio of (1) the number of pages of corporate AMT guidance to (2) the number of corporations subject to the corporate AMT. A meta-analysis shows that the ratio may reach infinity before the end of 2027, a point that can be called the corporate AMT singularity.

The corporate AMT retains its usefulness after that point, however, by exempting American corporations from pillar 2 and by increasing federal taxes collected from lobbyists, accounting professionals, and tax advisers. More states and localities may also impose their own versions of the corporate AMT.

title: Too Many Houses, Too Few People:  Demographic Optimism, Housing Oversupply, and Falling House Prices across Advanced Economies
affiliations: Wisconsin School of Business, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Seikei University, The University of Tokyo and Hitotsubashi University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: In population bonus periods, optimism about future housing demand fuels construction and price appreciation. In onus periods, official projections-anchored on earlier, more optimistic assumptions-can breed structural oversupply, rising vacancies, and prolonged price stagnation. We formalise this mechanism in a present-value and stock-adjustment framework and test it on panel data for 16 advanced economies, 1975-2019. Pooled mean-group estimates show a robust negative long-run association between projected ageing and real house prices: the projected old-age coefficient is significant in all estimation windows (-2.4 to-5.0); in the 1989-2019 window the projection-error component is larger still (-8.8), reflecting unanticipated demographic shortfalls. Interest-rate sensitivity is demographically conditioned: a one-percentage-point lower real rate is associated with house prices 2.4-3.7 percent higher in the youngest economies, with no detectable effect in the oldest. For ageing societies, policy should pair monitoring of projection errors with instruments that facilitate stock adjustment, rather than uniform monetary easing.
