detail.abstract: A Note on Perspective This paper examines competing schools of international relations thought-hegemonic stability theory, multipolarity, and small-state hedging-as analytical frameworks, not as normative endorsements of any government's foreign policy. Where the paper describes the interests, claims, or grievances of the United States, China, or Pakistan, it does so descriptively, to explain observed state behaviour, rather than to argue that any one power's role in the international system is normatively preferable to another's.

title: From Training to Print: Evidence on Peace Journalism as a Countering Violent Extremism Intervention in Pakistan

detail.title: From Training to Print: Evidence on Peace Journalism as a Countering Violent Extremism Intervention in Pakistan
detail.abstract:
Peace Journalism — a model of conflict reporting originally developed by Johan Galtung and subsequently
elaborated by Jake Lynch and Annabel McGoldrick, distinguishing war-and-violence-oriented reporting
from peace-and-conflict-oriented reporting — has increasingly been applied as a specific instrument of
Countering and Preventing Violent Extremism (C/PVE) programming, most rigorously documented in a
2024 study of Afghan journalist training that found a shift from a 23 percent to a 5 percent "War Journalism
quotient" and a 21 percent to 57 percent "Peace Journalism quotient" following training and mentorship. I
present here a Pakistani case — a 2016–17 USAID-funded activity I personally designed and managed,
working with the Bahawalpur Press Club in South Punjab — and evaluate it against this international
literature, using Alan Davis's influential three-tier framework for media development aid evaluation:
"benefit transferred" (knowledge conveyed in training), "benefit applied" (whether trainees changed their
actual published output), and "benefit beyond" (audience- and institution-level effects). Where much of the
peace journalism training literature has been able to document benefit transferred with more confidence
than benefit applied — a gap Lynch and Tiripelli's 2022 review of the field explicitly identifies — the
Pakistan case offers unusually concrete evidence of the latter: a Final Evaluation Report documenting
Bahawalpur Press Club's published columnist count rising from one to nine individuals, with twenty-two
specific, named, and dated articles published across regional and national outlets during and after the
training period. I argue that this concrete publication evidence, while lacking the systematic content-
analysis rigour of the Afghan comparative study, offers a rare and valuable contribution to a literature that
has more often had to rely on self-reported intention than documented published behaviour change.

title: Statelessness, Atrocity, and the Limits of International Law: The Rohingya Crisis Nine Years on A Legal and Policy Analysis, with Reference to The Gambia v. Myanmar

detail.title: Statelessness, Atrocity, and the Limits of International Law: The Rohingya Crisis Nine Years on A Legal and Policy Analysis, with Reference to The Gambia v. Myanmar
detail.abstract: Nine years after the August 2017 exodus, the Rohingya crisis remains one of the world's most protracted and least resolved instances of mass statelessness. This paper examines the legal architecture underlying the Rohingya's exclusion from Myanmar citizenship, traces the humanitarian and political trajectory of the crisis from the 1982 Citizenship Law to the present, and analyses the unfolding Gambia v. Myanmar proceedings before the International Court of Justice, where merits hearings concluded in January 2026 and a binding judgment is expected later this year. Drawing on current UNHCR, ACAPS, and ICJ data, the paper documents a refugee population that has grown from roughly 700,000 in late 2017 to more than 1.3 million by mid-2026, compounded by renewed displacement since 2024 and a deepening humanitarian funding crisis. The paper argues that international law has proven far more effective at documenting and characterising the Rohingya crisis than at resolving it: legal categorisation as genocide, however well evidenced, has not yet translated into citizenship restoration, safe repatriation, or accountability. The paper concludes with a revised six-point framework for durable resolution, updated to reflect the post-coup Myanmar context and the prospect of an ICJ judgment on the merits.

title: The Foundations of Economic Inclusion: Understanding the Measurements, Determinants and Barriers
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: The Foundations of Economic Inclusion: Understanding the Measurements, Determinants and Barriers
detail.abstract: Economic inclusion-defined as increasing the participation of economic agents in the formal economy-can bring many benefits to the economy. Yet, little is known about the measurements and determinants of economic inclusion and the barriers affecting economic inclusion. This article explores the concept of economic inclusion, the measurements, determinants and barriers affecting it. I show that economic inclusion can be measured using either the financial inclusion approach, the working population approach and the taxation approach. The identified determinants of economic inclusion are a level playing field for economic agents, income equality, political stability, equal opportunities, labour market flexibility, absence of market failure, financial inclusion, trust in government, active participation in business groups and economic associations, the availability of digital public infrastructure systems and internet coverage and usage. The study also identified several individual, societal, and structural challenges that may be encountered in advancing economic inclusion. I argue that economic inclusion, if it can be achieved, will build strong connections with people, communities and the formal economy. The starting point is to infuse the consciousness of economic inclusion into policymaking, policy design, private sector innovations and people's everyday interactions.

title:
Designing Sub-National Economic Policy:

The Sindh Domestic Commerce Policy and the Institutional Fragmentation Problem

detail.title:
Designing Sub-National Economic Policy:

The Sindh Domestic Commerce Policy and the Institutional Fragmentation Problem
detail.abstract: Sub-national economic policy-making in Pakistan operates within a specific structural constraint that is often under-examined in the policy documents themselves: the sheer density and fragmentation of the regulatory architecture any single reform must navigate. I examine here the Sindh Domestic Commerce Policy and Action Plan, developed in 2023–24 under the EU-funded GRASP project, as a case study in sub-national economic policy design within exactly this constraint. The policy, prepared through extensive stakeholder consultation involving the Department of Industries and Commerce, Sindh's Investment Department, the Karachi and Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, and other public and private actors, documents that approximately 35 distinct laws and regulations govern the conduct of business in Sindh, with registration and compliance responsibilities distributed across at least seven separate provincial agencies — the Directorate of Labour, the Sindh Employees' Social Security Institution, the Excise, Taxation and Narcotics Control Department, the Board of Revenue, the Sindh Building Control Authority, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Water and Sewerage Board — in addition to federal registration requirements. I argue that this institutional fragmentation, rather than any single named barrier, constitutes the domestic commerce sector's binding constraint, and examine the policy's proposed responses — a dedicated Legal Reforms Cell, a Commerce and Trade Promotion Committee chaired by the provincial minister, and a Warehouse Receipt Financing mechanism piloted in Sindh as early as 2015–16 — against this diagnosis. Drawing on my direct experience commissioning and coordinating this policy process across the province's senior bureaucratic and political leadership, I offer a practitioner's account of what sub-national economic policy design requires when the problem is not the absence of good ideas, but the sheer number of institutional actors any single idea must pass through to become practice.

title: Mission Anchoring: The Fixed Point in a Volatile World
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Mission Anchoring: The Fixed Point in a Volatile World

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: Organizations seeking to create impact over long periods must continually adapt to shifting political, economic, technological and social conditions, and doing so requires a fixed point of reference that does not change with them. This article argues that mission anchoring-the identification and maintenance of a stable, non-negotiable purpose that guides decisions such as methods, structures, partnerships, programs, products, services and operating models evolve-is a foundational capability of organizations designed for enduring impact, whether nonprofit or for-profit in form. The article defines nonnegotiable purpose and examines the mechanisms by which purpose is protected in practice including guardrails that subject new opportunities to mission-impact assessment, governance practices that include standing board review of purpose alignment and stakeholder feedback that surfaces inconsistencies early. The article further argues that endurance requires organizations to identify what they will refuse to become, converting abstract values into explicit refusal points that survive leadership transitions, and concludes by considering purpose discipline during scarcity, when the willingness to contract before surrendering identity, made possible by earlier investments in resilience, reveals whether mission anchoring is genuine or merely rhetorical.

title:
When the Secretariat Becomes the Directorate:

Institutional Design for Sindh's Department of Industries and Commerce

detail.title:
When the Secretariat Becomes the Directorate:

Institutional Design for Sindh's Department of Industries and Commerce
detail.abstract: The institutional strengthening study analysed in this paper was authored, on its technical substance, by Dr Nasir Javed, engaged as an independent consultant under a UN International Trade Centre (ITC) consultancy agreement, as part of the EU-funded Growth for Rural Advancement and Sustainable Progress (GRASP) project-a companion assignment to the Sindh Domestic Commerce Policy examined in a related paper in this series. My own role was to conceive and commission this institutional review, hire and manage the consultant, oversee the assignment budget, organise the Public-Private Dialogue sessions that tested the proposed reforms against stakeholder feedback, and coordinate directly with the Sindh Minister for Industries and Commerce, the Chief Secretary, the Secretary of the Industries and Commerce Department, and the Chairman of the Planning and Development Board. This paper draws on that vantage point to analyse the study's institutional design choices against comparative public administration theory; the underlying technical diagnosis is Dr Javed's work, properly credited throughout.

title: The Dagger - The Human Story Hidden Inside Mathematical Symbols
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: The Dagger - The Human Story Hidden Inside Mathematical Symbols
detail.abstract: This paper examines the sociology of mathematics through the lens of one of its smallest but most revealing symbols: the dagger notation (†) used for the conjugate transpose, or adjoint operator. It explores how this single typographic mark emerged not simply from mathematical necessity, but from the deeper human story of symbols, institutions, disciplinary traditions, and communities struggling to describe reality. Mathematics presents a beautiful paradox. Its truths appear to reach beyond humanity, yet its language carries unmistakable human fingerprints. From Galileo's mathematical universe, Newton and Leibniz's competing calculus notations, Euler's symbolic consolidation, Hamilton's quaternions, Cayley's matrices, Hermite's complex forms, Hilbert's search for foundations, and Dirac's quantum notation, mathematics evolves through a continuous conversation between reality and the human mind. The dagger becomes an artefact of this journey. It reminds us that transformation is incomplete without reflection. Every movement from one space to another demands a return question: what has changed, what has been preserved, and what remains unknown? Extending this insight into infrastructure and complexity, the paper argues that modern appraisal systems often struggle because they inherit powerful instruments of compression without equivalent instruments of reflection. The challenge is not simply reducing uncertainty. It is building systems capable of learning from the unknown.

title: Defining the Transaction in Transactional Economics

detail.title: Defining the Transaction in Transactional Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: This paper offers a concise definition of the transaction as the core unit of observation in Transactional Economics. At its simplest, a transaction is a completed and identifiable swap or transfer of mutually recognised value between distinct economic actors. In the ordinary market form, the seller or provider transfers a product, service, ownership position, access right, or other recognised value to the buyer or receiver, who settles the received value with money or another recognised form of value. The paper distinguishes this principal idea from broader economic changes such as production, extraction, valuation changes, internal accounting entries, and the mere creation or extinguishment of claims and obligations. Monetary and non-monetary transactions are treated as the main classes, while control positions, obligations, and observability are retained as descriptive dimensions. The purpose is to provide a simple, academically defensible, and operationally useful foundation for Transactional Economics, Gross Transaction Product, and transaction-based fiscal applications.

title: Value Co-Creation Challenges in the Cis-Lunar Economy: The Case of Moonraker in the NASA CLPS Program
affiliations: and

detail.title: Value Co-Creation Challenges in the Cis-Lunar Economy: The Case of Moonraker in the NASA CLPS Program
detail.abstract: The purpose of this descriptive, embedded single-case study (Yin, 2018) is to illustrate the distinctive features of co-creation and to discuss the concept’s application by presenting these issues within the unique context of Moonraker, a U.S.-based start-up in the New Space sector. This study addressed barriers that limit optimal value generation among stakeholders, particularly the insufficient inclusion of customers and external actors in current value constellation models. The study contributed knowledge to the Cis-lunar Economy Conceptual Framework (CLEF), which integrates key aspects such as policy and governance, sustainability and ethics, innovative business models, and technological advancement across seven interconnected domains of the cis-lunar economy. Using an embedded single-case study design, the study collects data via semi-structured interviews with company stakeholders, archival records, and document analysis. This multi-source approach allowed for triangulation and a nuanced understanding of organizational practices, challenges, and strategic responses during mission execution. Content analysis identified thematic patterns related to project management, innovation, and ecosystem dynamics. Findings showed that while Moonraker exhibits agility and technological innovation, it faces significant challenges, including financial reliance on government contracts, technical setbacks in lunar landings, and a lack of formalized management plans. The study highlighted the crucial interplay among CLEF’s dimensions and emphasized the need for diversified customer engagement, robust governance to create sustainable value, and for New Space ventures to adopt formal project management plans and prioritize co-creation with private customers to ensure long-term viability. Future researchers can apply CLEF to other start-ups to deepen the understanding of value creation in the New Space economy.

title: The Theory of Delegated Inertia: A Dynamical-Systems Model of Autonomy-Capability Traps in Emerging-Market Global Capability Centers

detail.title: The Theory of Delegated Inertia: A Dynamical-Systems Model of Autonomy-Capability Traps in Emerging-Market Global Capability Centers
detail.abstract: Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in emerging markets, especially India, frequently remain support-oriented execution units for years despite explicit intent from global headquarters (HQ) to grant them greater strategic autonomy. This paper develops a formal dynamical-systems theory explaining why autonomy delegation can stall even when both parties desire it. We build a three-variable continuous-time model of GCC capability C(t), HQ-granted autonomy A(t), and HQ trust τ (t), grounded in absorptive-capacity theory and the organizational competency trap. We derive equilibria, comparative statics and local stability analytically on a smooth invariant region, and corroborate them with full numerical integration and an illustrative population simulation anchored by secondary emerging-market industry data. The system is bistable: a low-capability dependency trap and a high-capability independence equilibrium coexist, separated by an unstable capability threshold that is a saddle. We prove the trap is locally stable for all admissible parameters and that the independence equilibrium is locally stable at every regular high-capability crossing. Increased HQ intervention ("help") strictly raises the tipping threshold-a formal cost-of-help mechanism. Distinguishing developmental coaching from substitutive takeover intervention refines this result: shifting a fixed quantity of help toward coaching strictly lowers the threshold, so the governance prescription is to redesign help, not merely to reduce it. For a fixed forced-autonomy intensity, escaping the trap requires an intervention sustained beyond a critical duration. The paper is a theory-building contribution; structural parameters are not estimated from firm-level data, and propositions are stated with the field data required to test them.

title: From Digital Industrial Relations to Internal Marketing: How Digital Employee Engagement Shapes Customer Experience and Brand Perception

detail.title: From Digital Industrial Relations to Internal Marketing: How Digital Employee Engagement Shapes Customer Experience and Brand Perception
detail.abstract: Through the introduction of new communication channels, data-driven workflows, and remote work arrangements, digitalization has completely changed the field of industrial relations (IR). Instead of using the conventional IR focus on compliance and conflict, this analysis reframes these developments via the perspective of Internal Marketing (IM) theory. IM views workers as "internal customers," whose drive and commitment to company objectives influence the value that is eventually provided to external clients. This paper proposes an integrated framework that links digital HR practices to employee engagement, service quality, customer satisfaction, and brand perception by synthesizing evidence on digital human resource (HR) tools (self-service HR information systems, AI-enabled performance and learning systems, internal social platforms, and remote-work technologies) and internal marketing mechanisms (communication, empowerment, training, and rewards). It does this by drawing on a systematic review of peer-reviewed and industry literature published between 2010 and 2026. According to the review, digital HR tools that are seen as helpful and used in conjunction with organizational trust (Hima et al., 2025) as well as those that are made to customize feedback (Diatmono, 2026) consistently increase engagement. The relationship between communication and job satisfaction is mediated by internal marketing strategies, especially empowerment (Bunea et al., 2025). Higher service quality and downstream customer loyalty are consistently linked to engaged, well-supported employees (Omagor et al., 2012; Gallup, 2020). The article ends with managerial suggestions for coordinating HR and marketing operations, theoretical contributions to internal marketing and branding literature, and future study directions on cross-cultural moderators and the moral implications of employee data use.

detail.abstract: Does language reshape what people eat? This paper identifies the causal effects of Mandarin proficiency and dialect distance on household food consumption in China, separating a human-capital "modernization channel" from a cultural-capital "local-network channel." Using three independent micro-datasets, the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS 2010 and 2014), the China Labor-force Dynamics Survey (CLDS 2014), and the China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS 1989-2015), we employ a three-layer identification strategy, with each layer relying on different identifying assumptions: two-stage least squares (2SLS) in the CFPS, instrumenting Mandarin proficiency with family language and county Mandarin share; an Atkin (2016)-style cross-dialect migrant design in the CHNS with community-by-wave fixed effects; and a bilingual dose-response analysis in the CLDS. Mandarin proficiency raises per-capita food expenditure by 13.85% and lowers animal-oil use, a pattern that replicates across datasets. Within the same communityyear, cross-dialect migrants consume 0.93 fewer food types and 0.65 percentage points less protein energy than local residents and take roughly thirty years to assimilate; a 1989 direct-recall item shows that only 49.4% of cross-province migrants retain home foodways, against 90.7% of non-migrants. We also report a cautionary null: province-level Mandarin penetration appears strongly correlated with dietary diversity but loses all significance once province fixed effects are added, signaling ecological-fallacy risk in crossprovince studies. An Ashenfelter-Krueger correction further shows that the OLS-2SLS gap is partly classical measurement-error attenuation, with an implied reliability ratio of 0.27-0.66. Mandarin promotion thus accelerates dietary modernization while potentially eroding dialect-encoded local food knowledge, implying scope to coordinate language and nutrition policy under the "Greater Food Vision.

title: Can Large Language Models Improve Scheduling Policies? Evidence from Queueing Networks, Job Shop Scheduling, and Ride-Hailing Dispatch
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong, The University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Management Sciences, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Industrial Engineering & Operations Research (IEOR) and City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Management Sciences

detail.title: Can Large Language Models Improve Scheduling Policies? Evidence from Queueing Networks, Job Shop Scheduling, and Ride-Hailing Dispatch
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted growing attention in operations management because of their distinctive ability to process task descriptions, constraints, and candidate solutions expressed in natural language. In this study, we examine whether LLMs can improve scheduling policies. We introduce LLM4SCHEDULE, a two-stage framework for LLM-assisted scheduling policy improvement, in which the LLM is used as an offline policy optimizer to help design and refine compact executable policies. In the first stage, an LLM generates multiple compact scoring-policy templates, each equipped with an admissible parameter space and an executable policy interface. Candidate templates are then checked for feasibility, semantic consistency, and executability, evaluated on a small batch of rollouts, and filtered to select a validated template for further refinement. In the second stage, the selected template is tuned through simulation feedback: candidate policies are evaluated via rollouts, numerical performance metrics and reasoning traces are stored in a history buffer, and the LLM iteratively proposes parameter updates. The final policy is evaluated on out-of-sample instances and can be deployed without invoking the LLM at runtime. We conduct extensive numerical experiments in three representative scheduling domains: queueing network control, job-shop scheduling, and ride-hailing dispatch. The results show that LLM4SCHEDULE improves upon direct LLM prompting and achieves performance competitive with selected learning-based approaches. In settings with explicit mathematical structure and well-established theoretical heuristics, standard heuristic policies can still achieve the best performance. However, in more realistic settings where mathematical assumptions are less explicit, LLM4SCHEDULE performs particularly well, suggesting that LLMs can help interpret and adapt to diverse practical scenarios. These findings indicate that LLMs are most useful as complements to operations research modeling and simulation-based policy refinement, especially when organizations have access to simulators or digital twins but lack well-tuned problem-specific heuristics. Taken together, the framework offers a practical way to incorporate language-based reasoning into scheduling policy development while preserving operational reliability.

title: The Predictive Customer Equity Framework (PCEF): Integrating Machine Learning, Structural Econometrics, and Latent Affective State Variables for Enterprise Valuation in Retail

detail.title: The Predictive Customer Equity Framework (PCEF): Integrating Machine Learning, Structural Econometrics, and Latent Affective State Variables for Enterprise Valuation in Retail
detail.abstract: Traditional methodologies for calculating Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) are predominantly retrospective and linear, treating retention as a stochastic process decoupled from internal organizational latency and the latent psychological states of the consumer. This paper introduces the Predictive Customer Equity Framework (PCEF), a multidisciplinary structural model that redefines customer portfolios as dynamic enterprise financial assets. By integrating deep learning architectures that continuously parse unstructured data streams with structural econometric discounting, we isolate a novel key variable: the Intrinsic Loyalty Coefficient (Λᵢ). This coefficient dynamically quantifies three latent affective state dimensions, specifically identity alignment, cognitive inertia, and satiation vulnerability, without direct or intrusive survey elicitation. The macro model further incorporates two internal firm constraints, the Data Hygiene Coefficient (αdata) and the Enterprise Transformation Index (βops), to capture operational drag. Through an empirical simulation study tracking 10,000 consumers over a 24-month horizon under competitive pricing shocks, we demonstrate that omitting internal operational modifiers and latent affective state vectors leads to structural mispricing of customer equity, frequently overvaluing opportunistic segments by more than 130 percent. Sensitivity analyses across seven parameterization scenarios confirm the directional robustness of this result. We provide mathematical optimization proofs confirming that maximizing Predictive Net Customer Equity (PNCE) yields superior long-term equilibrium net margins compared to traditional price-elasticity marketing models, offering a rigorous framework for strategic capital allocation.

title: Robots Went Where Workers Aged. Did AI? Demographic Labor Scarcity and the Direction of AI Adoption in Europe

detail.abstract: Industrial robots diffused fastest where middle-aged manual workers were scarce (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2022). Does artificial intelligence follow the same demographic logic? Using Eurostat enterprise surveys (2021-2025, 32 European countries, 11 industries), I interact national demographic scarcity with industry-level occupational AI exposure under country-wave and industry-wave fixed effects. Two margins pull in opposite directions. Workforce aging predicts higher AI adoption in exposed industries-about 1.5 percentage points per standard deviation pair, a tenth of the mean-with no counterpart for pre-AI technologies and timing that coincides with the post-2021 generative-AI wave. Scarcity of young tertiary-educated workers, the labor AI most directly substitutes for, predicts lower adoption: complementarity in deployment dominates substitution. The evidence comes from an interaction design supported by fertility-history instruments, randomization inference on the exposure assignment, and concentration in cognitive AI technologies with null placebos; it is best read as strong suggestive evidence rather than definitive causal estimation. The offsetting margins explain why the raw aging-AI correlation across countries is flat. The evidence is consistent with factor scarcity directing technology adoption only when the scarce factor is not also the technology's operator.

title: Tabular Foundation Models for Discrete Choice Estimation
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - Leeds School of Business and University of Colorado at Boulder

detail.title: Tabular Foundation Models for Discrete Choice Estimation
detail.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) generate predictions on structured data via in-context learning, without task-specific estimation. We ask whether TFMs can be effectively applied to discrete choice, a central demand estimation framework in marketing and operations, and find that directly applying TFMs yields limited performance. The gap is structural: TFMs assume row-independent observations, whereas discrete choice is inherently set-valued and subject to persistent consumer preference heterogeneity. We propose a reformulation that encodes both choice-set dependence and individual heterogeneity within a row-based learning framework. Evaluated on a yogurt scanner panel, individual-level heterogeneity encoding is the dominant driver of predictive accuracy. The best reformulation outperforms hierarchical Bayesian estimation by 8% in holdout log-likelihood and 3.6% in hit rate, running 16 times faster, a practical advantage for large-scale demand estimation. The advantage is largest in the medium-data regime (10-40 purchase occasions per consumer), where parametric Bayesian shrinkage most distorts estimates for atypical consumers. Fine-tuning on population choice data provides additional gains for consumers with shallow purchase histories, where in-context learning has limited individual-specific signal to condition on. These results establish a principled approach for applying foundation models to consumer choice problems more broadly.

title: Who Shares Data? Bounded Rationality and Strategic Disclosure in Data Markets *
affiliations: and

detail.title: Who Shares Data? Bounded Rationality and Strategic Disclosure in Data Markets *
detail.abstract: Privacy regulation relies on informed consent, delegating consumer protection to consumer choice. But the payoff to sharing depends on how firms use data and on who else shares, so disclosure is a strategic decision, and consumers differ in their ability to reason through it. This paper studies how bounded rationality changes the welfare consequences of transparency-based privacy regulation. We model data disclosure as a simultaneous strategic game in which a consumer's payoff depends on both firm use of the data and the composition of the pool that agrees to share. We estimate a cognitivehierarchy model using a data-sharing study fielded through the Dutch LISS panel, in which 3,598 respondents rated their trust in nine organizations and made a real decision whether to share their data with academic researchers. The estimates imply substantial heterogeneity in strategic sophistication: most consumers do not fully internalize the strategic consequences of disclosure, and beliefs about downstream data use differ sharply across organizations. We then evaluate a transparency policy that improves consumers' understanding of disclosure and shifts the population toward higher cognitive sophistication. The policy generates a direct welfare gain for previously naive consumers by correcting their disclosure mistakes, but it also induces adverse selection in the disclosure pool, lowering realized payoffs through an equilibrium channel. This sorting creates a privacy externality whose extent is bounded by the cognitive distribution. Whether transparency increases average welfare, therefor,e depends on the joint distribution of cognitive types and data values in the population.

title: Industry 4.0/5.0 Evolution: When Operational Implementation Goes Hand in Hand with Business Model Innovation
affiliations: University of Strasbourg and University of Strasbourg - Faculty of Economics and Management, University of Strasbourg - Bureau of Economic Theory and Application (BETA)

detail.title: Industry 4.0/5.0 Evolution: When Operational Implementation Goes Hand in Hand with Business Model Innovation

declarations.funderStatement: Thierry Burger-Helmchen has benefited from the support of the ECO-INNOVATE ANR-24-CE26-7829 project managed by Sophie Bollinger (University of Strasbourg) and from the support of the Fondation de l’Université de Strasbourg through the research project AOC “Agilité Organisationnelle et Créativité”

detail.abstract: This paper examines the shift from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 as implementation moves beyond operational efficiency toward business model innovation. Building on research on digital transformation and business models, we propose a process framework that links operational implementation stages (preparation, implementation, and operation), to increasing degrees of business model innovativeness (captured through sensing, seizing), and transforming. The framework is illustrated through a longitudinal single-case study of Henkel, based on archival evidence covering the period from 2013 to 2023. The findings show that business model change is progressive rather than immediate. Early investments focus on digitization, experimentation, and local pilots that primarily enhance efficiency within the existing business model. As connectivity, integration, and routinization expand across plants and functions, firms reorganize value creation and value delivery through data-driven coordination, automation, new roles, and governance mechanisms, while value capture changes remain more limited and emergent in the available evidence. The transition toward Industry 5.0 introduces human-centric, sustainability, and resilience priorities, which reinforce the need to redesign processes, decision rights, and performance indicators.

title: Reciprocal Deposit Networks and Funding Stability
affiliations: and Quantitative Supervision and Research - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

detail.title: Reciprocal Deposit Networks and Funding Stability
detail.abstract: We study banks' participation in reciprocal deposit networks and their financial stability implications. Our results show banks increasingly participate in these networks, with reciprocal deposit growth positively correlated with lagged uninsured deposits. Using daily Fedwire data, we provide first evidence that reciprocal deposits improve overall-not just deposit-funding stability during the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) crisis. Using unique multi-network membership data, we identify key drivers of network participation. Our novel data and findings advance understanding of how banks use network-based arrangements to manage funding risk, with implications for both deposit insurance policy and network design.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) infrastructure within telecommunications networks has exposed a fundamental gap in existing network management frameworks. Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), the de facto standard for network element monitoring since RFC 1157 (1990), provides no native support for monitoring AI accelerators, GPU clusters, high-bandwidth interconnects such as NVLink and InfiniBand, or AI workload telemetry. This paper proposes AI-MIB: a new Management Information Base extension that defines a standardised OID tree for AI infrastructure management within the SNMP framework. AI-MIB is designed to operate alongside existing OSS/BSS systems in telecommunications environments, preserving backward compatibility with SNMPv3 while extending the framework's scope to cover GPU health, accelerator interconnect metrics, AI workload performance indicators, and energy consumption-all critical parameters for operators deploying AI at the network edge, in Radio Access Networks, and in data centre environments. The proposed MIB tree is aligned with TM Forum data models and OpenConfig YANG schemas to facilitate integration with modern telecom orchestration platforms.

title: Managing Operational Flexibility of Wind-Storage Systems Under Uncertainty: A Singular Stochastic Control Approach
affiliations: Tianjin University of Finance & Economics, Tianjin University of Finance & Economics, Tianjin University of Finance and Economics, Tianjin University of Commerce - School of Management and Tianjin University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Managing Operational Flexibility of Wind-Storage Systems Under Uncertainty: A Singular Stochastic Control Approach
detail.abstract: The increasing penetration of wind power heightens the necessity of energy storage management. This study considers the dynamic operational management of battery energy storage systems (BESS) under price uncertainty, formulating the sponsor's decision as a singular stochastic control problem. First, we develop a unified framework for BESS operational flexibility that integrates a single charging strategy (CS), a single discharging strategy (DS), and a combined charging and discharging strategy (CDS) to analytically derive the intervention timing and target capacities. Subsequently, we rigorously characterize optimal policies under different cost structures, distinguishing the core differences between monotonic and non-monotonic convex battery costs. Furthermore, we show that despite incurring dual operational costs, the CDS expands the intervention region and yields strictly higher payoffs compared with the CS and DS. Finally, validating our theoretical model based on China Datang, we propose that for batteries with extreme costs, sponsors should consider the CS at low initial capacities, the DS at near-full capacities, and the CDS at moderate capacities. Comparative statics analysis demonstrates that exacerbated market uncertainty and operational frictions magnify the hysteresis effect, substantially delaying market interventions. Crucially, we uncover a profound cross-cost asymmetry: an escalation in charging costs counterintuitively amplifies the discharging payoff. This study provides valuable insights to help sponsors effectively manage BESS operational flexibility and realize optimal payoffs.

detail.abstract: Sustainable supply chains require analytical methods that explain how firms adapt supplier relationships under disruption while balancing resilience, resource efficiency, and environmental exposure. This study develops an agent-based network simulation and supply network analytics model to examine how selective supplier rewiring may shape sustainable supply network resilience. The model represents firms as autonomous agents embedded in a directed logistics supply network. Agents adjust sourcing ties under disruption using decision rules based on supplier dependency, relational embeddedness, supplier reliability, capacity, network proximity, and supplier sustainability performance. The simulation is used as a theory-elaborating computational experiment rather than as an empirical validation design. Under the specified model assumptions, selective rewiring generates patterns of more balanced structural adaptation than random or unconstrained supplier switching. Local sourcing decisions produce measurable changes in density, clustering, modularity, path length, recovery, and sustainability exposure. The sustainability-constrained scenario illustrates how supplier replacement rules are associated with a higher simulated sustainability profile of active ties while preserving recovery performance under the specified model assumptions. The study contributes to supply chain analytics by linking micro-level supplier adaptation rules with macro-level network transformation. The results should be interpreted as simulation-based patterngeneration outcomes that require future empirical validation using real-world longitudinal supply network data.

detail.abstract: Regulators worldwide are drafting prohibitions on dark patterns—interface designs that exploit consumer biases—without quasi-experimental field evidence on how they change consumer behavior. This study evaluates what is, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive e-commerce statute to name and prohibit six distinct dark-pattern practices—South Korea's amended E-Commerce Act (effective February 2025)—using 484,085 app reviews of 72 apps over 42 months and a dictionary-plus-LLM complaint classifier validated against independent human coders (κ = .79). Contrary to the preregistered compliance hypothesis, complaints about the six banned design types did not decline after enforcement: relative to within-app placebo topics they rose 44% (p = .001), with no dose–response improvement among high-exposure apps and no rating gains. Instead, deception-inference language jumped 55% in the quarter the law passed and remained elevated, and complaints spilled over to legal scarcity tactics. Effects survive nine robustness tests, including exclusion of the 0.4% of complaints mentioning the law and placebo-date permutations. The findings identify publicized prohibition as a market-level persuasion-knowledge intervention and expose a measurement paradox: complaint-based enforcement metrics systematically understate—and can invert—regulatory success.

detail.abstract: Partisan theory predicts that left-wing governments resist delegating public services to private providers. I test this prediction with a sharp regression discontinuity design in close Brazilian mayoral elections contested between left and non-left candidates over the 2016 and 2020 cycles (3,601 races), combining party ideology scores from the Brazilian Legislative Survey with a comprehensive registry of public–private partnership (PPP) and concession contracts. Electing a left-wing mayor has no detectable effect on the number of contracts signed during the term: the preferred estimate is 0.003 contracts (95% CI −0.023 to 0.035), robust to bandwidth, kernel, polynomial order, alternative ideology classifications, and outcome definitions. Equivalence tests rule out effects of 0.034 contracts or larger, and Bayes factors provide moderate evidence for the null. Even at the peak of Brazilian polarization, fiscal, institutional, and capacity constraints appear to crowd out partisan preferences in complex contracting decisions.

title: Self-Publishing versus Publisher-Backed Publishing in Digital Game Distribution
affiliations: Washington University in Saint Louis, John M. Olin Business School, Students, Washington University in Saint Louis - John M. Olin Business School and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Self-Publishing versus Publisher-Backed Publishing in Digital Game Distribution
detail.abstract: Independent game developers must choose a publishing mode: whether to self-publish or work with a publisher that can amplify demand. We build an analytical model in which the developer's effort is unobservable and the publishing mode is endogenous. Publisher commercialization capability raises the marginal return to quality, but revenue sharing weakens the developer's quality-enhancing effort. We show that equilibrium price, effort, and publishing mode are characterized by two cutoffs for the publisher's capability and for the game's baseline quality relative to development cost. The developer self-publishes when publisher capability is low but the game's baseline quality-cost index is high enough to support standalone entry; publisherbacked publishing arises once publisher capability is sufficiently high. Using profit sharing as a diagnostic benchmark, we show that some publisher-backed releases fail to arise under revenue sharing because of incentive misalignment rather than insufficient surplus creation. We further show that publisher capability is more effective when it complements game quality rather than merely expands exposure, and that revenue sharing can distort not only developer effort but also game selection. We provide suggestive descriptive evidence from the Steam PC games market during 2015-2025. The patterns are directionally consistent with the theory: Publisher-backed publishing is positively associated with developer ability and generally positively associated with baseline quality, while launch prices are positively associated with baseline quality, developer ability, and publisher capability.

detail.abstract: SummaryBackground In 2020, our thoracic anaesthesia department changed its default strategy for eligible thoracoscopic procedures from planned tracheal intubation and one-lung ventilation to a structured non-intubated pathway. We assessed programme reach, airway escalation, and perioperative outcomes compared with the preceding intubated cohort.Methods In this single-centre retrospective before-and-after policy cohort, we screened 1019 thoracoscopic procedures performed in France between Jan 1, 2015, and Dec 31, 2025. The eligible source population comprised 480 pre-policy intubated procedures, 480 post-policy intended non-intubated attempts, and 19 post-policy planned intubated procedures for predefined contraindications. Primary implementation outcomes were completion without airway escalation, supraglottic-airway support without intubation, and tracheal intubation. Exploratory recovery comparisons used 1:1 propensity-score matching.Findings Among 480 intended non-intubated procedures, 456 were completed without airway escalation (95·0%, 95% CI 92·7–96·8), 22 required supraglottic-airway support without intubation (4·6%, 2·9–6·9), and two required tracheal intubation (0·4%, 0·1–1·5). Matching retained 385 pairs and achieved absolute standardised mean differences below 0·10 for all measured covariates. Hypotension occurred in 40/385 (10·4%) non-intubated and 72/385 (18·7%) historical intubated patients (conditional odds ratio 0·50, 95% CI 0·32–0·77); postoperative nausea and vomiting occurred in 33/385 (8·6%) and 78/385 (20·3%), respectively (0·41, 0·26–0·64). Median hospital stay was 3 days (IQR 2–4) versus 4 days (3–5).Interpretation A departmental non-intubated thoracic pathway was deliverable in selected patients, with supraglottic-airway support functioning as an infrequent intermediate rescue step and tracheal intubation rarely required. Favourable matched recovery associations should be interpreted as policy-period signals rather than causal effects because anaesthetic strategy and calendar era were inseparable.

title: Digital Servitization and Operational Productivity: Resolving the Paradox Through Capability Mechanisms in EU Manufacturing
affiliations: South China University of Technology, University of Warwick - Warwick Manufacturing Group and University of Warwick - Warwick Manufacturing Group

detail.title: Digital Servitization and Operational Productivity: Resolving the Paradox Through Capability Mechanisms in EU Manufacturing
detail.abstract: Evidence on whether digital servitization (DS) improves manufacturers' operational productivity (OP) remains contradictory, a tension known as the digital servitization paradox. Drawing on the sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring microfoundations of the Dynamic Capability Theory (DCT), we resolve this paradox by identifying the capability mechanisms through which DS affects OP and the boundary conditions under which these mechanisms operate. Specifically, we examine the non-linear DS-OP relationship, the moderating role of risk sensing capability (RSC), and the mediating role of resource integrating capability (RIC) across heterogeneous innovation environments. Combining text-mined data from firms' annual reports with financial data from Orbis, we construct a panel of 335 EU-15 manufacturing firms over 2017-2023. We measure DS using expert-validated text-mining and OP using input-oriented Data Envelopment Analysis. Hypotheses are tested using System GMM, with formal U-shape tests and extensive robustness checks. We find a significant U-shaped relationship between DS and OP: an initial productivity dip from organisational friction, followed by gains as DS matures. RSC steepens this U-shape, while RIC also exhibits a U-shaped association with DS and partially mediates the DS-OP relationship. These patterns hold only in innovation-leading and R&D-intensive contexts; elsewhere, DS exerts no significant effect on OP. Managers should treat DS as a staged transformation and expect an initial productivity dip rather than abandon it prematurely. Investment in RSC and RIC pays off mainly where digital infrastructure and R&D base already exist. Policymakers should pair digital incentives with investment in national innovation systems. To our knowledge, this is the first study to jointly identify the mechanisms and boundary conditions of the DS-OP relationship. Theoretically, we resolve the digital servitization paradox as a U-shaped adjustment process driven by distinct capability mechanisms. Empirically, we confirm the U-shaped adjustment process and identify national innovation capability and R&D intensity as boundary conditions. Methodologically, we offer a replicable archival measure of DS capturing digital-service fusion.

detail.abstract: For much of the twentieth century, mainstream financial theory rested on a deceptively clean premise: that people invest rationally, markets price assets correctly, and any deviation from fair value gets corrected almost instantly by profit-seeking arbitrageurs. The Efficient Market Hypothesis gave this premise theoretical form, and for decades it shaped how economists, fund managers, and regulators understood financial markets. What it could not explain, however, was why bubbles form and collapse with such regularity, why the same investors make the same mistakes through successive market cycles, and why the arrival of more information technology has not made markets noticeably calmer. This paper approaches those questions through the lens of behavioural finance, a field that takes seriously the psychological reality of how people actually make financial decisions rather than how a perfectly rational agent would. The study draws on two parallel bodies of evidence: a structured questionnaire survey of 107 respondents conducted in April 2026, and a synthesis of twenty-five peer-reviewed studies and reports published between 2018 and 2025. Together, these sources paint a coherent picture of a retail investor population that is more active, more connected, and more emotionally engaged with markets than any previous generation, and that carries the same cognitive vulnerabilities that researchers have documented for decades. Survey results show that 70.1% of respondents use social media as an investment input, 63.6% would buy more of a stock that has already fallen 20%, 57.9% have invested at least once due to Fear of Missing Out, and 67.1% rate their stock-picking ability above average. Against the backdrop of secondary evidence showing that 89% of Indian retail options traders lost money over three years and that the most active quintile of investors earns roughly 6.5 percentage points less per year than a passive index fund, these self-reported patterns have measurable financial consequences. The paper situates these findings in real-world market episodes including the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, the Indian cryptocurrency collapse of 2022, and the extraordinary post COVID surge in Indian retail trading, and concludes with practical recommendations for regulators, platform designers, and investors.

title: The Security Council-General Assembly Divide: Article 24(I) and the Limits of Collective Security in the Maintenance of International Peace A Legal and Policy Analysis

detail.title: The Security Council-General Assembly Divide: Article 24(I) and the Limits of Collective Security in the Maintenance of International Peace A Legal and Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the institutional and legal relationship between the United Nations Security Council and the General Assembly in the maintenance of international peace and security, with particular attention to the interpretive scope of Article 24(I) of the UN Charter. It argues that while Article 24(I) confers "primary responsibility" upon the Security Council and authorises it to act on behalf of the wider membership, this primacy is not absolute. The Charter, supplemented by the General Assembly's 1950 Uniting for Peace Resolution and the International Court of Justice's 1962 advisory opinion in Certain Expenses of the United Nations, preserves a residual-and at times decisive-role for the General Assembly when the Security Council is rendered inactive by the veto. Drawing on the contrasting institutional responses to the Kosovo crisis (1999-2008) and the Ukraine crisis (2014-present), the paper demonstrates that this dual-track architecture, while procedurally sound, produces inconsistent outcomes that often track the interests of the Permanent Five rather than a coherent doctrine of collective security. The paper concludes that meaningful reform of the veto power, rather than incremental reliance on the Uniting for Peace mechanism, is required if the United Nations is to discharge its founding mandate credibly in a multipolar international order.

title: Strength in Numbers: Ethnic Group Size and Economic Development
affiliations: and

detail.title: Strength in Numbers: Ethnic Group Size and Economic Development
detail.abstract: Do agglomeration gains operate within ethnic groups? We study whether larger coethnic populations lead to higher levels of group economic development in the long run. To identify this effect, we exploit the arbitrary partition of African ethnic homelands caused by the Scramble for Africa, which generated exogenous variation in the size of the same ethnic group across adjacent countries. We find that a 10 percent increase in pre-colonial population causes a roughly 2 percent increase in nighttime light density today. Results are robust to a battery of geographic controls and to alternative measures of pre-colonial population, including machine learning-based predictions and land area. We trace the mechanisms using geocoded survey data: larger populations have generated denser urban agglomerations, better transportation infrastructure, and a greater likelihood of hosting the national capital. Residents of larger-group territories have attained higher education, work in more formalized and occupationally diversified labor markets, exhibit better anthropometric outcomes (a marker of cumulative long-run development), and display fertility patterns consistent with a demographic transition. These gains are place-based rather than ancestry-specific. While larger groups are also more politically powerful, absolute population size (economic gains of scale) outperforms population share (relative political power) in predicting long-run development.

title: Unpacking Board Model Choice in Europe: A Multi-Methods Approach
affiliations: Fordham University School of Law and European University Institute (EUI)

detail.title: Unpacking Board Model Choice in Europe: A Multi-Methods Approach

publicationDetails.detailsText: Fordham Law Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: The design of corporate governance structures is a major topic in the legal and management literature; yet there is little research on what accounts for the choices that companies make. This paper aims to contribute to this under-researched topic by examining the fundamental choice between corporate board models, notably, between one-tier and two-tier models (i.e. companies with or without a supervisory board). Based on data from 147,000 firms across fourteen European countries, it finds that the choice of board model is associated with the composition of the company's shareholders, personal characteristics of the company's directors and different types of firms. In addition, the paper exemplifies the benefits of applying a multi-method approach, being based on a combination of regression and random forest analysis, as well as qualitative interpretation. The random forest analysis, which had not yet been applied to this question, was found to be particularly helpful in understanding, by means of exploratory research, a large number of possible reasons, forms of non-linearity and other complexities.

title: Capital Costs, Reinsurance, and the Price of Climate Risk
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Iowa - Department of Finance,  and

detail.title: Capital Costs, Reinsurance, and the Price of Climate Risk
detail.abstract: In catastrophe-exposed insurance markets, a large share of what homeowners pay reflects the cost of correlated tail risk. Local insurers cannot diversify these losses on their own and instead transfer them to globally diversified reinsurers, but reinsurance is expensive and volatile. We study a regulatory reform that decreased the capital cost of reinsuring tail risk. After the cost decrease, reinsurance use expanded by 25%, the reinsurance market became less concentrated, and the model-implied price of reinsurance fell by a third. By reducing required capital, the reform also increased insurers' exposure to reinsurer non-payment risk. We show this dramatically impacted the primary insurance market in hurricane-exposed areas of Florida: additional insurers entered and the cost of insuring wind risk fell sharply. To quantify welfare, we estimate an equilibrium model of the Florida wind-insurance market. The model implies that the reform reduced treated insurers' marginal cost of supplying wind coverage by about 10% and lowered equilibrium premiums by about 14%. Counterfactual simulations imply consumer-surplus gains of $186 per household per year, split roughly equally across direct cost pass-through, strategic markup adjustment, and expanded product availability. Our results imply that capital costs required to cover tail events, over and above average losses, meaningfully contribute to consumers' premiums and that policies that reduce those capital costs can decrease prices and improve availability for homeowners insurance.

title:
Leadership Without Formal Authority: A Practitioner's View from Pakistani Development Governance 
Applying Goleman's Leadership Styles and Nye's Smart Power to Multi-Stakeholder Public Sector Practice

detail.title:
Leadership Without Formal Authority: A Practitioner's View from Pakistani Development Governance 
Applying Goleman's Leadership Styles and Nye's Smart Power to Multi-Stakeholder Public Sector Practice
detail.abstract: Leadership theory has been developed and tested overwhelmingly in corporate and Western institutional contexts, where leaders typically possess clear hierarchical authority over the people they lead. I argue in this paper that leadership in donor-funded, multi-stakeholder development programming-the context in which most public sector reform in countries like Pakistan actually occurs-presents a structurally different problem: the effective leader routinely has little or no formal authority over the government officials, community representatives, private sector actors, and donor counterparts whose cooperation is essential to programme success. Drawing on Daniel Goleman's typology of six leadership styles and Joseph Nye's concept of "smart power"-the combination of hard and soft power appropriate to contextalongside fifteen years of my own direct experience leading teams and coalitions ranging from 23 international consultants to over 50 field staff across Pakistani provincial governance and post-earthquake recovery programmes, I argue that relationship-based leadership styles (affiliative, coaching, and democratic) function as load-bearing infrastructure in these contexts, not merely a stylistic preference, precisely because positional authority cannot substitute for the trust required to coordinate across genuinely independent institutional actors. I also examine the gendered dimension of this leadership environment, updating the discussion with current data: while Pakistan's 2024 civil service examination results show women winning a record 48 percent of entry-level allocations, women remain only 5 to 6 percent of the existing federal and provincial bureaucracy and fewer than 1 percent of officers who reach the civil service's highest rank-a considerably steeper "leaky pipeline" than the roughly 11 percent Fortune 500 CEO representation now observed globally. I conclude that leadership development for public sector and development contexts needs its own body of applied practice, distinct from corporate leadership literature, centred on the specific problem of achieving results through actors a leader cannot command.

title: The Audacity of Calling Women the "Weaker Gender" A Psychological Exploration of Women's Resilience, Sacrifice, and Social Strength

detail.title: The Audacity of Calling Women the "Weaker Gender" A Psychological Exploration of Women's Resilience, Sacrifice, and Social Strength

declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is based on a qualitative conceptual analysis informed by published literature and observational insights. No human participants were recruited, no personal or identifiable data were collected, and no interventions were conducted. Accordingly, formal institutional ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Women have historically been described as the "weaker gender," despite their significant psychological, emotional, and social contributions across families, communities, and societies. This paper critically examines that stereotype through a psychological lens by synthesizing established theories of resilience, self-efficacy, emotional labour, caregiving, feminist psychology, and post-traumatic growth. Using a qualitative conceptual approach informed by observational insights and existing scholarly literature, the study explores how women demonstrate strength through perseverance, caregiving, adaptation, leadership, and emotional resilience in everyday life. Rather than viewing strength solely in terms of physical capability, the paper argues that psychological resilience and sustained social contribution provide a broader and more meaningful understanding of human strength. The findings challenge long-standing gender stereotypes and highlight the need for greater recognition of women's resilience in psychological research, education, workplace policy, and public discourse.

detail.abstract:
Provider credentialing is typically treated as an administrative prerequisite, a compliance step to clear before
a clinician can see patients and generate revenue. This report argues that framing understates the problem.
Drawing on data published by CAQH, the American Medical Association, the Association for Advancing
Physician and Provider Recruitment, AMN Healthcare, NSI Nursing Solutions, and healthcare M&A market
research, this report traces how credentialing delays propagate through ten distinct dimensions of
organizational performance: revenue, provider productivity, patient access, payer relationships, operational
efficiency, physician satisfaction, competitive advantage, organizational growth, EBITDA and margins, and
enterprise value.

For a healthcare executive, credentialing is not a back office function to be minimized in a board discussion.
It is a variable that touches nearly every line of the income statement, and increasingly, the multiple a buyer
is willing to pay at exit. This report introduces the Koru Credentialing Impact Matrix, an executive
framework for locating which of these ten dimensions represent visible, already managed risk, and which
represent quiet, unmanaged exposure, and closes with the Koru Engagement Model for acting on that
diagnosis.

title: Occupational health technologies as a driver of innovation: A model for the control of psychosocial risks and the improvement of organizational efficiency in the automotive industry
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Occupational health technologies as a driver of innovation: A model for the control of psychosocial risks and the improvement of organizational efficiency in the automotive industry
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the role of occupational health management technologies as a strategic resource for strengthening the control of psychosocial risks and improving organizational efficiency in Tier 1 automotive suppliers. The research was conducted using a quantitative, exploratory, observational, and cross-sectional approach, considering a sample of 120 senior management leaders from Tier 1 automotive suppliers. Structural equation modeling (SEM), a robust statistical technique, was used to validate the proposed hypotheses and examine the relationships between the study variables. The results show that occupational health management technologies positively influence the control of psychosocial risks by facilitating more effective monitoring, prevention, and follow-up systems. Furthermore, it was found that the proper management of these risks has a significant effect on organizational efficiency, as the reduction of work-related stress and psychosocial burdens leads to better performance and greater employee productivity. A direct impact of these technologies on organizational efficiency was also confirmed. As its main contribution, the study integrates occupational health, psychosocial risks and organizational performance into an innovative and replicable model, demonstrating that psychological health is a strategic factor for the competitiveness and sustainability of Tier 1 companies in the automotive sector.

title: Hedging as Prepositional Focusing: A Learnable-Theoretic Account of the Persuasive Sweet Spot

detail.title: Hedging as Prepositional Focusing: A Learnable-Theoretic Account of the Persuasive Sweet Spot
detail.abstract: Recent work in consumer psychology shows that hedging, the linguistic marking of uncertainty, is not uniformly bad for persuasion. Oba, Boghrati, and Berger demonstrate across seven studies that hedges combining high-likelihood language (e.g., "should," "likely") with personal perspective (e.g., "I believe," "in my opinion") occupy a communicative sweet spot: they signal speaker confidence and thereby increase persuasive impact relative to both unhedged absolutes and low-likelihood, impersonal hedges. This article develops that finding further using the apparatus of Learnable Theory: the Learnable Enhanced Bhaskarian Ontology (LEBO), prepositional focusing and defocusing, the Complementary Semantic Distance Index (CSDI), the umbra cone construct, and Differenza Inversa (Inverse Difference), as set out across the Learnable Theory corpus (Magni, Marchetti, & Alharbi, 2023, 2024, 2025). We argue that hedging is not best understood as a graded modulation of propositional certainty. It is an act of prepositional attachment that occurs at the Learnable stratum of LEBO, not at the Actual or Empirical strata: a speaker either anchors a claim to a locatable subject, the self, or leaves it ownerless. The corpus defines Differenza Inversa as an intrapsychic operator for reinterpreting autobiographical memory. We extend it here, as a proposed analogy rather than a documented application, to the interpersonal resolution of an unmarked speaker/claim attribution. The compensating relationship between surface hedging and relational ownership is one observable signature of that proposed analogy, not evidence the source construct has already established. We also show that the sweet-spot register carries a predictable CSDI signature, Self-Actualization-Positive, and that this signature produces an umbra cone effect: it shadows Safety-domain content in the same message. Maximal persuasiveness and maximal disclosure end up pulling in opposite directions. We derive seven testable propositions from this account, discuss its implications for organisational communication, leadership discourse, and human-AI meaning-making, and close with the framework's limitations and boundary conditions. Seven original figures accompany the argument: a typology of hedge types (Figure 6), an anatomical diagram of the umbra cone construct (Figure 2), a process model linking utterance to persuasive outcome (Figure 5), a diagram distinguishing Differenza Inversa's source construct from its proposed extension to hedging (Figure 3), and a model of the human-AI coupling behind AI-generated hedges (Figure 7).

title: African Exchanges Linkage Project: An Empirical Assessment
affiliations: Tulane University

detail.title: African Exchanges Linkage Project: An Empirical Assessment
detail.abstract: The African Exchanges Linkage Project (AELP), launched on November 18, 2022, connects seven major African equity exchanges (BRVM, Egypt, Johannesburg, Morocco, Nairobi, Nigeria, and Mauritius) through a shared platform intended to deepen integration and improve market efficiency. Using daily index data from January 2016 through early 2026, we test for changes in pairwise integration, directional information flow, and weak-form efficiency around the AELP launch. Dynamic conditional correlations among the seven markets are essentially flat across the launch, and the only structural break we detect in the integration index predates the launch by more than five years.We find evidence of improved weak-form efficiency. The aggregate change in the runs statistic across the seven markets is significant at the 1\% level and the result survives global factor controls and COVID-window exclusion. The Granger causality network among the seven markets contracts substantially after the launch, with the number of significant pairwise directional links falling from 25 to 10, a result that runs counter to the AELP's stated objective of deepening cross-border price discovery. The findings parallel the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect experience, where informational efficiency improved without measurable change in aggregate co-movement. The post-launch contraction in the directional network has no direct SHHKConnect parallel and is a novel contribution of this study.

title: Organized Volunteering and Civic Agency Among University Students in Bangladesh: A Comparison of Volunteers and Non-Volunteers

detail.title: Organized Volunteering and Civic Agency Among University Students in Bangladesh: A Comparison of Volunteers and Non-Volunteers
