detail.abstract: Organized volunteering is often assessed through participation or behavioral outcomes, leaving uncertainty about whether volunteers differ from non-volunteers in perceived civic capacity. This study examined the association between organized unpaid volunteering and civic agency among 280 undergraduates from eight purposively selected Bangladeshi universities, with equal volunteer groups. Civic agency was measured using a Bangla-adapted 16-item scale. Group differences were tested with independent samples t tests, followed by ordinary least-squares regression and cluster-robust analyses. Volunteers reported higher overall civic agency than nonvolunteers, t(278) = 3.75, p < .001, d = 0.45. The adjusted association remained positive, B = 0.260, SE = 0.067, β = .223, p < .001, and significant under CR2 and wild cluster bootstrap procedures. The findings support distinguishing civic agency from participation in voluntary action and suggest that universities and volunteer organizations should evaluate how volunteer roles involve responsibility, collaboration, feedback, and opportunities to contribute.

title: The Effect of Regulatory Harmonization on Cross-Border Labor Migration: Evidence from the Accounting Profession
affiliations: The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Humboldt University of Berlin - School of Business and Economics, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: The Effect of Regulatory Harmonization on Cross-Border Labor Migration: Evidence from the Accounting Profession
detail.abstract: The paper examines whether international regulatory harmonization increases cross-border labor migration. To study this question, we analyze European Union initiatives that harmonized accounting and auditing standards. Regulatory harmonization should reduce economic mobility barriers, essentially making it easier for accounting professionals to move across countries. Our research design compares the cross-border migration of accounting professionals relative to tightly matched other professionals before and after regulatory harmonization. We find that international labor migration in the accounting profession increases significantly relative to other professions. We provide evidence that this effect is due to harmonization, rather than increases in the demand for accounting services during the implementation of the rule changes. The findings illustrate that diversity in rules constitutes an economic barrier to cross-border labor mobility and, more specifically, that accounting harmonization can have a meaningful effect on cross-border migration.

title: AI Capital Allocation and Governance: A Portfolio Model

detail.title: AI Capital Allocation and Governance: A Portfolio Model
detail.abstract: Most AI governance asks whether a system is safe enough to run. This paper asks whether a workload is worth funding, how much risk it adds to the firm’s AI portfolio, and whether the whole book stays inside a limit the firm has agreed to carry. It sets out a model that treats AI activity as a portfolio of distinct investments, each valued against a named financial driver, costed on a fully burdened basis, and judged by its marginal, correlation-aware contribution to a risk budget grounded in the board’s appetite and the firm’s capacity to absorb loss, with an absolute floor no expected return can buy through. The portfolio framing is now widely urged; the machinery underneath it is the contribution.

reference: In The Nature of Corporations (Jonathan Hardman, Billie Lythberg, Christoph Van der Elst & Susan Watson eds., Edinburgh Univ. Press forthcoming 2027; SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 744
title: The Incorporation Ritual
affiliations: Hofstra University - Maurice A. Deane School of Law and Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law

detail.title: The Incorporation Ritual

contentType.other: The Nature of Corporations (Jonathan Hardman, Steve Kourabas, Billie Lythberg, Christoph Van der Elst, & Susan Watson eds.) (University of Edinburgh Press) (forthcoming 2027)

publicationDetails.detailsText: In The Nature of Corporations (Jonathan Hardman, Billie Lythberg, Christoph Van der Elst & Susan Watson eds., Edinburgh Univ. Press forthcoming 2027
SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 744
publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
What makes a business worth the corporate form? From Rome through England and America, the corporate form was granted only after an assessment that the undertaking served a governmental or public interest. Free chartering ended that inquiry. Any lawful purpose now qualifies, and nothing distinguishes on the merits the undertakings that deserve corporate personhood from those that do not. So what marks the distinction?

This chapter locates it in the formalities of incorporation itself and argues that those formalities are far older and stranger than they appear. The forms, filing fees, and certificates that incorporators navigate today are the secularized descendants of rites that once called cities and corporations into being through fire, prayer, and the turning of sacred earth.

Drawing on Arnold van Gennep's rites of passage, Victor Turner's account of liminality, and Roy Rappaport's insight that rituals do not describe transformations but perform them, the chapter traces a ritual lineage from the founding of Rome to the secretary of state's filing window. It runs through Fustel de Coulanges' reconstruction of the sacred fire, Pope Innocent IV's persona ficta, the asset partitioning of Benedictine monasteries and the Cluny charter of 910, the coniuratio by which medieval guilds constituted themselves through mutual oath, and the royal charters of the first joint stock companies. A survey of initiation rites across five traditions establishes that the pattern is structural rather than culturally specific.

Read this way, the state seal is a ritual blessing, fiduciary duties are secularized oaths, and administrative dissolution is the extinguished hearth. The chapter's sharpest claim concerns what free chartering discarded. Stripping the ceremony from incorporation also stripped the inquiry the ceremony once carried, leaving a procedure that still transforms status but no longer asks whether the transformation is deserved. Recovering incorporation's ritual character restores a lost recognition: creating a new legal person is a momentous act, not paperwork.

title: Continuity, experiential knowledge transfer, and the architecture of public health institutional memory in the context of health crises
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt - University of Zurich, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Zurich

detail.title: Continuity, experiential knowledge transfer, and the architecture of public health institutional memory in the context of health crises
detail.abstract: Background: Public health institutions often document crisis response, but documentation alone doesn’t ensure that experience remains accessible and usable for future preparedness.  Objectives: This study examined how experiential knowledge in Swiss public health is stabilized, transferred, or lost across institutional boundaries after a health crisis subsides, and what supports institutional continuity over time.  Methods: This exploratory mixed-methods study combined a survey administered during a workshop on public health knowledge transfer with subsequent semi-structured interviews. The study included 32 survey respondents and three qualitative interviews. It assessed perceived mechanisms of experiential knowledge transfer, perceived effectiveness of these mechanisms, professional experience, and perceived challenges to institutional continuity.  Results: Respondents reported limited insight into how experiential knowledge is secured and transferred (M = 2.56, SD = 1.22), and perceived knowledge transfer as poorly organized and effective (M = 2.22, SD = 0.83). Academic studies (M = 3.03), internal reports (M = 3.00), and standard operating procedures (M = 2.97) were rated highest. More frequent use of transfer mechanisms was associated with greater perceived effectiveness (β = 0.45, p = .02). Qualitative findings showed reliance on informal networks and identified fragmentation, staff turnover, weak coordination, and separation of research and practice as challenges to continuity. Conclusions: Institutional memory in Swiss public health requires information systems, documentation and sustained organizational practices that preserve, interpret, and translate experience into future preparedness and decision-making. Embedding structured reflection, debriefing, and cross-institutional exchange into routine preparedness work may reduce reliance on individual staff members and support continuity after crises.

title: Appealing to Emotion or Reason?The Interaction Effect between Streamer Language Style and Purchase Motivation on Purchase Intention
affiliations: Hohai University, Hohai University and Hohai University

detail.title: Appealing to Emotion or Reason?The Interaction Effect between Streamer Language Style and Purchase Motivation on Purchase Intention
detail.abstract: In livestreaming, streamers’ linguistic style is a key communication factor influencing consumers’ purchasing intention. The current research on the language styles of streamers focuses on demonstrating the advantages of a single language. The study takes the elaboration likelihood model (ELM) as a theoretical framework to explore the mechanism of different streamers’ language styles (emotional vs. rational) on consumers’ purchase intention in different contexts. Through three scenario-based experiments, the results show that: (1) Streamers’ language style and consumers’ purchase motivation interact to influence purchase intention; rational language facilitates in improving purchase intention under utilitarian motivation, while emotional language performs better under hedonic motivation; (2) Processing fluency mediates the interaction effect between language style and purchase motivation. The findings are crucial for understanding how streamers’ language style and consumer motivation interact to influence purchase intention, providing significant implications for livestreaming.

title: Masked Erosion: Visible Performance and the Hidden Decay of Reproductive Stocks

detail.title: Masked Erosion: Visible Performance and the Hidden Decay of Reproductive Stocks
detail.abstract: Many systems are judged by fast performance flows although future performance depends on slower reproductive stocks. This paper studies masked erosion, in which output is sustained by hidden use intensity that also depletes the stock. In a population of systems, current performance loads positively on both stock and persistent intensity, while future stock loads positively on stock and negatively on that intensity. We show that the covariance between current performance and future stock crosses zero at a unique horizon: performance is informative before it becomes misleading. Technological change can create or compress this crossing by altering the production-reproduction mapping, while institutions continue to apply rules adapted to the old regime. The resulting mismatch is an aggregate signal failure: local choices may be rational, but no decentralized actor naturally owns the population-level crossover. The framework implies that stock, use intensity, and renewal must be measured separately from current output.

title: Guarding the Wrong Door: Autonomous Economic Agents, Emergent Capability Convergence, and the Absence of a Defendant When Catastrophe Is Assembled from Individually Benign Open Components

detail.title: Guarding the Wrong Door: Autonomous Economic Agents, Emergent Capability Convergence, and the Absence of a Defendant When Catastrophe Is Assembled from Individually Benign Open Components
detail.abstract: The dominant regimes for governing extreme risk in advanced artificial intelligence concentrate their attention on the frontier: the largest models, the highest training compute, and the small set of developers able to build systems that surpass human expertise. This paper argues that the most plausible near term path to catastrophic capability does not run through the frontier at all. It runs through an autonomous agent, operating under economic survival pressure, that repurposes and combines individually benign components drawn from open code repositories, model hubs, and research literature into a capability that exists in no single component and that no component author intended. Two of the three ingredients are established results that belong to other researchers and are not claimed here: the self-preservation disposition of contemporary models, and the deployed infrastructure of the autonomous agent economy. The contribution is the third ingredient and its union with the first two, namely emergent convergence, the composition of unrelated capabilities across authors who never coordinated, applied to the autonomous economic agent. The paper makes three further claims. First, the literature on unintended repurposing and dual use is deep but treats the problem as a property of a single model or a single actor, not as emergent composition across many. Second, the frontier oriented governance instruments cannot detect this path because every one of them presumes a chokepoint, a point of creation or deployment at which a state can intervene, and the installed base of open weights models running on consumer hardware bypasses every such point. Third, and distinctively, the harm has no cognizable defendant: the secondary liability doctrine that governs dual use tools shields each component author under Sony and requires purposeful, culpable inducement under Grokster, and in this scenario there is no inducer, no manufacturer of the assembled capability, and no intending author of the combination. The paper closes by arguing that only a monitoring discipline organized around integration surfaces could detect this class of risk, and is candid about that discipline's limits.

title: The Value Dynamics of Data Assets: From Production to Coordination
affiliations: Imperial College London

detail.title: The Value Dynamics of Data Assets: From Production to Coordination
detail.abstract: Classical asset theory expects productive assets to depreciate: machines wear out, knowledge diffuses, and informational advantages erode. Yet valuable assets in the contemporary economy behave differently. Behavioural datasets can gain value through use, appreciate with age, and become more valuable when combined. This paper develops a framework for explaining these dynamics. First, it defines data assets and models their value as a contest between appreciation mechanisms, including accumulation, flywheels, combinatorial linkage, and temporal rarity, and depreciation mechanisms, including temporal decay, diffusion, and displacement. This yields a taxonomy of eight data-asset types distinguished by the temporal behaviour of their value. Second, the paper adds fungibility as a third axis to the classic rivalry and excludability classification of goods, producing the REF Framework: an eight-position property space through which data assets move as they are collected, combined, enclosed, and deployed. Third, it shows that firms able to exploit these dynamics do not merely accumulate data or automate decisions. They build feedback loops through which realised outcomes become future inputs for coordination, learning, and resource allocation. We identify this recursive conversion of outputs into inputs as the defining organisational feature of "Datalist" coordination. The framework explains why data-rich markets tend to concentrate, why possessing data differs from mastering its use, and why value accrues to those controlling the infrastructures and capabilities that refine data, rather than to the people whose activity generates it. It follows that assigning data ownership to individuals leaves the locus of appropriability largely untouched.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Quadratic Voting Counterfactuals in Token-weighted Governance: A Case Study of the Arbitrum DAO

detail.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Quadratic Voting Counterfactuals in Token-weighted Governance: A Case Study of the Arbitrum DAO

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None, this is an independent study - conducted with nobody but myself, and data & resources available online for free, with no attachments,
declarations.funderStatement: No one, this is an independent study, using resources on the internet.

detail.abstract:
Most decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) use a 1-Token-1-Vote rule, allowing capital ownership to translate directly into governance power. This paper evaluates how a Quadratic Voting (QV)-inspired square-root reweighting counterfactual would affect voting outcomes in the Arbitrum DAO. For this, a time-paginated pipeline was developed to retrieve approximately 850,000 off-chain Snapshot vote records across fifteen of the DAO's highest-turnout proposals where each participating wallet's token-weighted voting power was replaced with its square root, and the proposal outcomes were recalculated.


The results reveal extreme concentration of voting power, with a mean Gini coefficient of approximately 0.9950 among active participating wallets. In some proposals, the ten largest participating wallets or delegates collectively controlled as much as 86.87% of the total voting weight. Consequently, square-root reweighting changed the winning outcome in four of the fifteen proposals (26.7% of this purposively-selected, high-turnout sample), demonstrating that these outcomes were sensitive to the distribution of voting power across wallets. Its effect on victory margins was heterogeneous: margins widened in six proposals and narrowed in nine, with changes ranging from a 55.90-percentage-point expansion to a 37.76-percentage-point contraction. Notably, all four outcome reversals involved funding, grants, security expenditure, coalition financing, or related resource-allocation decisions. These findings suggest that square-root reweighting can alter both the magnitude and direction of token-weighted governance outcomes by reducing the relative influence of highly concentrated token holdings.

title: The Closed Evidentiary World: A Warranted-Corpus Architecture for Research-Grade Language Models

detail.title: The Closed Evidentiary World: A Warranted-Corpus Architecture for Research-Grade Language Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

keywords.keywords: warranted corpus; epistemic warrant; provenance; retrieval-augmented generation; abstention; claim-level filtration; institutional epistemology; language models; generative asymmetry

detail.abstract: Frontier language models fail in a way research libraries do not. Where a catalogue or database returns a null result for an absent record, a generative model is structurally disposed to return fluent language, manufacturing an information-like artifact in place of an honest absence. This paper names that difference the generative asymmetry and treats it, rather than hallucination in general, as the specific problem for research-grade factual generation. It proposes a bounded remedy: a warranted-corpus architecture in which a model’s affirmative factual claims are confined to a versioned baseline of atomic claims that identifiable scholarly, archival, and legal institutions have graded as warranted, while the model’s linguistic freedom is left intact—an open linguistic world governing a closed evidentiary world. The proposal is deliberately narrow. It is not a theory of truth, a policy program, or a cure for hallucination in open-domain conversation; it is a theoretical architecture for constrained factual generation, grounded in institutional epistemology. Its central commitment is to filter claims rather than documents, admitting warranted assertions wherever they occur and excluding unwarranted ones even from otherwise reputable sources. The paper distinguishes truth, warrant, and admissibility; specifies a four-layer architecture with an explicit abstention rule; locates the design against prior traditions it integrates but none of which imposes its hard output boundary; and, reflexively, applies its own evidentiary discipline to its own composition.

title: When GenAI Scores Become Measures: A Design Framework for Digital Trace Research
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Management,  and University College London - Institute of Health Informatics

detail.title: When GenAI Scores Become Measures: A Design Framework for Digital Trace Research
detail.abstract: GenAI can readily turn digital traces into scores for concepts that researchers cannot observe directly. Yet a stable score that predicts behavior may still measure the wrong thing. We develop Certified Generative Trace Measurement, a framework for testing whether a generated score captures its named concept rather than repackaging information researchers already observe. Three preregistered studies use four model families and 158,246 audited API records across 57,125 U.S. expenditure interviews, 110,747 de-identified ticketing orders, and 5,896 public GitHub pull requests. Three findings stand out. First, all 13 target scores are stable, but only 35 of 330 proposed uses predict behavior beyond information already shown to GenAI. Second, prediction does not reveal meaning: on GitHub, deliberately irrelevant scores predict outcomes as often as plausible scores, so none of the apparent successes qualifies as a measure. Third, in later expenditure data, treating every stable score as a measure falsely admits 70 of 90 uses; behavioral screening cuts that number to five, though it misses nine later signals. Even the best-performing score predicts behavior across models and time without proving its label. We derive five design principles for deciding when a GenAI-created score can enter analysis and when researchers must abstain. Generated scores should begin as measurement hypotheses, not measures.

title: The Costly Signal That Costs Nothing: Formal Apparatus, the Verification Premium, and the Audit of Machine-Generated Scholarship

detail.title: The Costly Signal That Costs Nothing: Formal Apparatus, the Verification Premium, and the Audit of Machine-Generated Scholarship

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

keywords.keywords: large language models; epistemology of testimony; costly signaling; research integrity; citation practice; preprint ecosystems; confabulation; verification cost; machine-assisted scholarship; Maestro Model

detail.abstract:
Scholarly apparatus is a costly signal: a document object identifier once implied a registrant and a fee. The inference from apparatus to verification was sound because apparatus was expensive. This essay documents what happens when the marginal cost of the form collapses and the inference does not adjust.

The evidence is three machine-generated documents on one subject, audited claim by claim. The most credentialed carries a named review protocol, forty-six references, and a DOI whose registrant prefix is the string 10.XXXX. Recomputed from its own printed parameters, it assigns one pair of market values to two different economic quantities, runs two inconsistent models of its headline figure and reports one, and states a session count roughly twice what its method generates. A limit central to its regulatory argument is wrong by an order of magnitude.

Three further layers are examined. An evaluator ranked the credentialed document highest on data credibility, citing a placeholder DOI and absent confidence bounds. A commissioned verification dropped an assigned item and corrected a claim only the author's prompt had implied. Three reviewers that endorsed this argument returned six undifferentiated scores, one reporting its own truncation as a manuscript defect and one deriving a quantity from a figure acknowledged to have no source.

The essay names the failure mode the formality gradient: the rise of a document's apparent warrant with its apparatus, absent any rise in the verification beneath it. It is distinguishable from hallucination, invisible to claim-level sampling, and hazardous to preprint infrastructures. Three remediations are proposed, none restoring apparatus as a proxy for verification.

title: Voluntary Certification and Project Choice
affiliations: Free University of Berlin (FUB) - School of Business & Economics, School of Economics, University of Edinburgh and

detail.title: Voluntary Certification and Project Choice
detail.abstract: We study how voluntary certification affects project choice when certifiers have market power. A monopolistic certifier charges a fee to verify returns generated by projects chosen by a continuum of ex ante identical agents. We show that the certifier optimally induces distortions in the agents' project choices if certification costs are high enough. In particular, the certifier induces a partial certification equilibrium under which certified agents disclose only high returns and choose projects that maximize the upside potential whereas uncertified agents choose cost-minimizing projects.

title: Thirteen Tank Cars of Tattoo Ink and the White Whale, Moby Dick: Tattooing, Meaning, and the Quantity Nobody Has Counted

detail.title: Thirteen Tank Cars of Tattoo Ink and the White Whale, Moby Dick: Tattooing, Meaning, and the Quantity Nobody Has Counted

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

keywords.keywords: tattooing; body modification; marking; totemism; legibility; depth psychology; Jung; Freud; tattoo ink; REACH; pigment migration; demographic prevalence; measurement uncertainty; Melville

detail.abstract:
Marking is a claim upon an interior the observer cannot inspect. A tattoo asserts something about the person who wears it — a lineage, a loss, a conviction, an ordeal survived — and it asserts this to observers who have no access whatever to the interior the claim concerns. This essay takes that structure seriously as an epistemological problem and follows it through four questions: what a tattoo asserts, who makes tattoos and against what, what the material is and where it goes in the body, and how much of it is used.

The first three questions have answers. Freud's account of totemism supplies the social condition the psychological readings presuppose: a mark carries authority because a community determines who may bear it, what relationship it records, and what prohibitions attend it. A reading built on Freud's structural model then distinguishes the impulse discharged onto the skin from the Ego's signature and from the Superego's compliance tattoo; a Jungian reading distinguishes the Persona display, worn to signal an identity not internally conferred, from the symbol that records work actually done. Verified survey data show tattooing more prevalent among women than men and among Black and Hispanic Americans than among White and Asian Americans, and show tattooing-as-statement cited more often by groups for whom institutional credential is less available — a pattern consistent with a substitution hypothesis that is advanced here as interpretation and is not established by the figures. Synchrotron mapping has established that pigment does not remain where it is placed: nanoparticles migrate by lymphatic drainage to regional nodes, which extends the relevant exposure from a local dermal question to a systemic one. European law restricts several thousand substances in tattoo formulations; United States law approves no color additive for injection into skin, so that an ink containing one is adulterated as a matter of law — a prohibition that has nonetheless gone essentially unenforced, which is a different thing from permission and is frequently reported as though it were the same.

The fourth question has no answer. This essay reconstructs the published consumption estimates from the parameters their own authors state, finds that they do not survive the arithmetic, and offers a bounded reconstruction, built on partly unverified inherited assumptions, with its uncertainty propagated rather than suppressed: somewhere between two railroad tank cars and thirty-five. A practice this ancient, this widespread, and this regulated has never been counted.

title: When Anyone Can Build, Who Evaluates? Use-Side Governance in AI Skill Ecosystems
affiliations: University of Washington - Department of Information Systems and Operations Management and INSEAD - Decision Sciences

detail.title: When Anyone Can Build, Who Evaluates? Use-Side Governance in AI Skill Ecosystems
detail.abstract: AI skills are shareable, reusable, task-specific instructions that AI agents interpret and execute to perform recurring workflows. They now circulate at scale through public repositories where anyone can publish or adopt one. Generative AI has lowered the cost of producing these artifacts far faster than platforms have developed standards for describing and verifying them, so users must judge what a skill does and whether to trust it from a listing alone. What governance work makes this abundant supply evaluable and usable? We study 49,332 skills from ClawHub, a public AI skill repository. Embedding the available skill specifications, we recover a functional taxonomy of the ecosystem that is only partly captured by the platform’s preset discovery vocabulary and labor-market skill labels. Free-text search often returns relevant candidates, but skill-detail pages leave users to locate or infer intended-use boundaries, validation evidence, and approval status from unstructured descriptions, revealing an evaluability gap between how skills are presented and the evidence users need before reliance. Creation does not translate into adoption: 94.8% of skills are dormant and the top 0.26% capture about half of installs. We develop these patterns into a theory of use-side governance: how artifact evaluation work is allocated and absorbed across platforms, organizations, and users, with platform curation and AI fluency as complementary capabilities. Task-level evidence from the Anthropic Economic Index, linked through a shared O*NET work frame, supports the role of AI fluency—evaluating rather than passively relying on AI outputs predicts higher task success. Generativity without evaluability produces abundance without usable supply. When anyone can build, platform governance should shift from attracting creators and expanding supply toward supporting effective evaluation and use.

title: Algorithmic Orchestration in Gig Work: How Information Restriction and Matching Coordination Improve System Efficiency
affiliations: University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management, Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California, University of Connecticut - School of Business and University of Southern California, Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Algorithmic Orchestration in Gig Work: How Information Restriction and Matching Coordination Improve System Efficiency

declarations.funderStatement: University of Connecticut Research Excellence Program Fund

detail.abstract: In gig economy platforms, matching is not only an allocation problem but also a governance problem: providing information about the task prior to matching can be attractive for workers but may reduce system-wide efficiency. We examine how platforms can reshape pre-match conditions, to improve efficiency. We use algorithmic orchestration to describe a form of governance configuration that coordinates decentralized workers by jointly restricting decision-relevant information and strengthening platform-directed matching coordination. We examine its impacts in the context of Uber's introduction of Personal Identification Number Match at LaGuardia Airport, which restricted drivers' access to trip information before matching and sequenced ride assignments through a platform-managed queue. Leveraging granular trip-level data with precise pickup locations and a quasi-experimental design, we find that algorithmic orchestration improved system efficiency, as reflected in a 4.50% reduction in rider wait times and a 9.86% increase in driver earnings. The effects are larger during high-demand periods and for trips ending in lowerincome areas, where pre-match screening is more likely to impede efficient matching. These findings demonstrate that matching systems serve not only as allocation tools but also as governance approaches that shape worker behavior before transactions occur. By shifting attention from post-task monitoring and incentives to governance choices that prevent choice and lead to random allocation, we contribute to the research on platform governance and algorithmic management by identifying pre-match governance as a distinct form through which platforms can balance worker autonomy with system-wide coordination efficiency in decentralized digital labor markets.

title: RAG Systems and the Illusion of Accuracy: Rethinking Attorney Competence Standards for Legal AI

detail.title: RAG Systems and the Illusion of Accuracy: Rethinking Attorney Competence Standards for Legal AI
detail.abstract: Legal AI tools marketed as "hallucination-free" continue to produce inaccurate legal analysis at rates incompatible with their marketing. This article examines why retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), the architecture underlying leading legal research platforms, reduces but cannot eliminate hallucination, and why the profession's regulatory response has misdiagnosed the resulting competence problem. The first preregistered empirical evaluation of these tools documents hallucination rates between 17% and 33% for products offered by LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters (Magesh et al., 2025), with theoretical work suggesting some hallucination rate is intrinsic to calibrated generative models (Kalai & Vempala, 2023). Current ethical guidance, including ABA Formal Opinion 512 and Florida Bar Opinion 24-1, instructs attorneys to verify AI output without acknowledging what this article terms the verification paradox: RAG's citations to authentic sources make its errors systematically harder to detect than the fabrications of general purpose chatbots, so the tools that appear most trustworthy demand the most sophisticated distrust. The article argues that compliance with Model Rule 1.1 therefore requires graduated technical competence keyed to RAG's specific, predictable failure modes, and it proposes a tiered verification framework in which the required depth of attorney verification scales with the weight the AI output carries in the legal task. The framework extends a principle this author has defended in the due process context: procedural safeguards for algorithmic systems must be calibrated to the reliance placed upon them.

title: Social Media Entrepreneurial Intention in Vietnam: The Antecedents of Personal Background and Psychological Beliefs in Becoming Influencers
affiliations: Vietnam Aviation Academy and Faculty of Commerce and Tourism of Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City

detail.title: Social Media Entrepreneurial Intention in Vietnam: The Antecedents of Personal Background and Psychological Beliefs in Becoming Influencers

publicationDetails.detailsText: Machine and Computing Technologies for Sustainable Development (MCT4SD 2025)

detail.abstract: This study examines the factors influencing Social Media Entrepreneurial Intention (SMEI) among influencers in Vietnam, where the digital economy and social commerce are rapidly expanding. We focus on two main groups of factors: (1) Personal Background, including Age, Gender, Experience, Entrepreneurial Education and Family Support; (2) Psychological Beliefs, based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), including Personal Attitudes, Subjective Norms and Perceived Behavioural Control. Data were collected from an online survey with 261 participants on social media platforms in Vietnam. The results indicate that Personal Attitudes, Subjective Norms, and Perceived Behavioural Control have a positive influence on Entrepreneurial Intention. Within the Personal Background group, significant differences are observed in Gender, Experience, and Entrepreneurial Education, while Age and Family Support do not have a statistically significant impact. This result suggests that psychological preparation, Experience through social media platforms, and Entrepreneurial Education play a more important role than Age or Family Support in the context of low-barrier social entrepreneurship. These findings provide practical value for policymakers and educational institutions in promoting entrepreneurship on social media.

title: Effects of Lottery Incentives for Influenza Vaccination: Evidence from a Large-Scale Randomized Trial and Causal Forest Analysis
affiliations: , Geisinger Health System, Geisinger Health System, Geisinger Health System - Bioethics Research, Geisinger Health System and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Economics, Finance, Accounting (EFA)

detail.title: Effects of Lottery Incentives for Influenza Vaccination: Evidence from a Large-Scale Randomized Trial and Causal Forest Analysis
detail.abstract: Financial incentives may encourage vaccination, but their cost-effectiveness depends on targeting patients who are most responsive. We conducted a randomized controlled trial with 57,579 adult patients in an integrated health system during the 2021–2022 influenza season. Patients with an upcoming appointment were randomized to a no-contact control, a simple reminder, a $1 cash incentive, or a scratch-off lottery ticket incentive worth up to $5,000. Any active intervention increased vaccination at the scheduled appointment by 2 percentage points (an 8% increase over the control mean) and by 1.5 percentage points over the full influenza season. The three active arms did not differ significantly, indicating that small financial incentives provided no additional benefit beyond a reminder. Using electronic health records and area-level characteristics, we used causal forests to estimate conditional average treatment effects. Predicted responsiveness varied substantially: patients in the top quartile were 3–4 times more likely to respond to incentives than those in the bottom quartile, whereas reminder effects were relatively homogeneous. These findings suggest that low-cost reminders can increase influenza vaccination, while machine-learning methods can help identify patients most responsive to small financial incentives.

title: Early Life Healthcare Access and Later-life Mortality: Evidence Using Openings of County Health Departments
affiliations: Austin Peay State University and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Early Life Healthcare Access and Later-life Mortality: Evidence Using Openings of County Health Departments
detail.abstract: This paper examines the long-term effects of early-life exposure to county health departments (CHDs), a public health initiative aimed at providing affordable healthcare access to disadvantaged and underserved areas during the early decades of the 20th century, on later-life longevity. We employ Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census and implement a difference-in-differences estimation strategy to compare the longevity of individuals exposed at different ages to the county-specific year of CHD establishment. We find that exposure to a CHD opening in the county of birth during fetal development and early years of life is associated with a 1-4-month increase in longevity. We observe considerable heterogeneity in the results, such that the effects are more concentrated among non-white individuals and individuals with lower-educated parents. Contemporaneous fertility and infant mortality data suggest reductions in infant mortality rates and increases in birth rates following CHD openings. Additionally, we find significant improvements in educational attainment, socioeconomic status, and income in early adulthood. We argue that enhancements in the fetal environment, improved fetal survival, and better early life health capital resulting from CHD exposure contribute to improvements in human capital during adulthood, with potential implications for later-life longevity.
